entries.title: New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill Calls for Her Lieutenant Governor to Resign
entries.summary: An ethics investigation found Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell harassed a staffer and violated ethics rules.
entries.content:
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill called for the resignation of her second in command, Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell, after ethics investigators concluded his behavior constituted sexual harassment and violated ethics standards.

A 61-page report by investigators for an outside law firm includes evidence that Caldwell sought a promotion for his girlfriend, brought guests to ticketed events without payment and told a female staff member that young women want "young sperm.”

Sherrill announced the findings Thursday on X and gave Caldwell “until tomorrow” to resign. The two were elected on the same ticket and took office in January.

“The Lieutenant Governor’s resignation is necessary and in the best interest of New Jersey residents,” she said. “The investigation found that the Lieutenant Governor engaged in serious, repeated violations of state policy and failed to uphold the responsibilities of his office.”

The report followed an anonymous complaint received by the governor’s chief ethics officer in May. Investigators with the law firm Lowenstein Sandler found Caldwell, 66, made the sexual remark after a staffer told him a friend was not interested in a relationship with the lieutenant governor.

Caldwell then remarked that the staffer and her friend “needed a man who was in a position to help them,” the report states, before going on to make additional crude statements.

The unnamed staffer told investigators the incident was “textbook sexual harassment" and caused her take measures to distance herself from Caldwell at work and to avoid traveling with him.

Caldwell denied making the comment, the report said, but investigators found his account lacked credibility given numerous similar incidents and contemporaneous documentation provided by the staffer.

Sherrill said the ethics violations persisted despite “multiple warnings and trainings.”

“The substantiated finding of sexual harassment is extremely troubling,” she said. “I’ve seen firsthand how a hostile culture can undermine everyone’s ability to succeed. It’s insidious and ruptures the trust within an organization.”

The report also found that Caldwell used his government email to seek a promotion for his girlfriend, who is a state employee, four days after receiving notice of the ethics investigation. He did not disclose their relationship in the communications, and the woman did not receive a promotion, raise or other benefits.

Investigators also found Caldwell routinely brought guests to ticketed events without payment, despite receiving guidance from ethics officials.

Caldwell did not immediately respond to The Washington Sun’s request for comment.

entries.title: Trump and Xi Toast to Mutual Cooperation at Opulent White House State Dinner
entries.summary: The guest list included more than 130 people, including tech executives and three Supreme Court justices.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping for a lavish White House state dinner Thursday night, pairing Chinese emissaries with American billionaires and government officials against the backdrop of ongoing trade and technology negotiations.

Dignitaries gathered in the East Room — which was draped in red linens and decorated with blossoms, dahlias, ranunculus and gold-plated silver — and heard the two state leaders’ toasts over glasses of Schramsberg “Blanc De Noir,” the same wine served during President Richard Nixon’s famous 1972 “Toast to Peace” in Beijing.

In his opening address, Trump called Xi and his delegation “truly amazing, outstanding people,” invited the group to tour the unfinished White House ballroom, and gifted Xi with a statue of a bald eagle that he said he designed himself along with first lady Melania Trump.

“As the leaders of our two nations,” Trump said, “President Xi and I both understand that we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we've never gotten along better.”

In his statements, the Chinese president broadly detailed the progress made since Trump’s visit to China in May, when the two leaders agreed to further bilateral ties. Xi and Trump had “sincere and in-depth exchanges,” the state leader said, and had reached “common understanding on many issues.”

“This has added new substance to the constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability,” Xi said, adding that “China and the United States must act as responsible major countries, meet the expectations of our peoples, keep pace with the trend of our times, and explore a new approach for major countries to get along with each other.”

Xi concluded his statements with a toast, lifting his glass to “the friendship of our two peoples.”

APTOPIX Trump Xi (1024x682, AR: 1.50)
The lengthy guest list included more than 130 people, bringing together executives with competing visions for AI governance — a running motif of this week’s summit — including OpenAI’s Sam Altman, who recently urged more international safeguards, and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, who reportedly lobbied Trump against national regulations.

Elon Musk was also listed as a guest, signaling a potential reconciliation after he and Trump had a public falling-out in June 2025. Earlier this month, Trump told Fox News he would not impede Chinese automakers who seek to build electric vehicles in the U.S. — a move that could encroach on Musk’s territory, as Tesla battles Chinese company BYD to lead the world in EV sales and production.

Trump Xi (1024x682, AR: 1.50)
Most reporters were not welcomed into the East Room for the meal, with the exception of a group of Fox News personalities, including Laura Ingraham, Bret Baier and Jesse Watters.

Chief Justice John Roberts and Trump-appointed justices Amy Coney Barrett and Brett Kavanaugh were also invited.

Trump Xi (1024x682, AR: 1.50)
Ahead of Xi’s entrance, a few moments of disorder took place. Outside the executive residence, White House staff turned away reporters from MS NOW and CNN from the arrival ceremony, as reporters were required to get preapproval by Wednesday night to cover the event. At the time, Trump’s ban on the outlets had not yet been lifted.

Protesters waiting for the Chinese motorcade chanted “free Hong Kong” and called for China to release political prisoners ahead of the dinner.

“CCP, your empire will fall! CCP, you’re not welcome!” some shouted.

Just after 7 p.m., Trump and the first lady greeted their Chinese counterparts and stood for photos in the newly renovated North Portico.

The two leaders ignored questions from reporters about Taiwan or artificial intelligence as they entered the White House. Trump also declined to answer whether he had asked Xi to free imprisoned Chinese activist Jimmy Lai, who was arrested and sentenced in 2020 for his role in organizing Hong Kong’s pro-democracy movement.

entries.title: All-DMV High School Soccer Players of Week 1
entries.summary: This week’s group features a lockdown defender from the Churchill boys and a potent goal scorer from the St. John’s girls.
entries.content:
This story is part of The Washington Sun’s All-DMV coverage. All-DMV is a new collaboration between The Sun, Fox5 DC, NBC4 Washington and WTOP News, aimed at covering the D.C. area’s best high school athletes. You can find past players of the week and more information about All-DMV here.

The first month of the soccer season was a busy one as local contenders jostled for position against division rivals to boost their resumes come playoff time. Here are six September standouts — three boys and three girls — whose performances earned them All-DMV Player of the Week:

Adiah Aahmez, Sophomore, Midfielder, Bowie

Aahmez has looked comfortable in a new role for a Bowie boys’ team that graduated 11 seniors from last year’s squad, six of whom went on to play collegiate soccer. The sophomore center midfielder picked up a goal and two assists as the Bulldogs scored three early victories against Mount Hebron, Bladensburg and Annapolis Area Christian.

Margaret Brault, Senior, Midfielder, St. John’s

Brault was the star of the St. John’s girls’ blowout win over Elizabeth Seton on Tuesday. She scored four goals in the victory, bringing her tally to six goals on the young season. Brault shines on both sides of the ball — the senior also provides tenacious defense for a Cadets team that’s looking to defend its Washington Catholic Athletic Conference crown.

“She’s constantly a threat, constantly looking to help build a play for her team, and one of those people that just has an immediate impact in the game,” St. John’s coach Allison Diaz said.

Tobi Falayi, Senior, Defender, Churchill

Falayi is the anchor of the Churchill boys’ stout defense. An all-state defender a season ago, Falayi’s constant defensive presence helped the Bulldogs to three shutout victories amid a five-game September winning streak. Their most recent victory came Wednesday in shutout fashion against Maryland Class 4A rival Whitman, an impressive result over a Vikings team that made the state finals last season.

Emery Gregory, Senior, Midfielder, Eleanor Roosevelt

Gregory has wasted little time finding her footing offensively for the Eleanor Roosevelt girls. The senior midfielder is already up to five goals and two assists for the Raiders, who scored an early 3-1 rivalry win over Bowie. The defending Prince George’s County champs also scored 5-0 tournament victories over Guilford Park and Bishop McNamara.

Ege Kirgiz, Senior, Forward/Midfielder, Potomac School

The Potomac School boys raced out to a 3-0 start, and Kirgiz was a big reason why. The left-footed senior picked up three goals and two assists for the Panthers, who took down Saint James (MD), St. Christopher’s and Episcopal. Kirgiz’s steady play as both a forward and midfielder gives coach Travis Beauchamp the ability to unleash him all over the field for the Mid-Atlantic Athletic Conference contenders.

Chloe Russ, Senior, Goalkeeper, Walter Johnson

If the Walter Johnson girls want to make a deep playoff run this season in a loaded division stacked with state title contenders, it’ll need strong defensive play. Russ, the Wildcats’ senior goalkeeper, has helped provide that so far — she didn’t let in a goal in her first three starts of the season. First-year coach Ilyes Ouldbrahim’s team picked up division wins in shutout fashion against Whitman and Quince Orchard.

entries.title: The Mystics Are Back in the Playoffs. Now They Want More.
entries.summary: They’ll be the No. 5 seed, set for a matchup with Atlanta, when the WNBA playoffs start on Sunday.
entries.content:
A funny thing happened in Capital One Arena on Thursday. Sydney Johnson’s record as head coach of the Mystics finally reached .500.

The team has won so much in his second year that it has been easy to forget how much they lost in his first year. Consider: The Mystics have known for weeks that playoff basketball will be happening in D.C. come late September. They have been the hottest team in the WNBA since the All-Star Break. Johnson has a legitimate case for Coach of the Year. Does it not seem that surely, surely, the coach must have already shed his losing record with the franchise? It does.

Yet it did not actually happen until Thursday, the final night of the regular season, with a 101-93 win over the Sky. The game helped clinch the No. 5 playoff seed for the Mystics. And it created a remarkable symmetry across Johnson’s two years in D.C.

In his first season with the young, rebuilding Mystics, Johnson led them to a record of 16-28. And in his second season with the still-young, very-much-rebuilt Mystics, he led them to a record of 28-16.

The results have completely flipped. Here is .500: Every loss this core experienced last year has been balanced by a win this year. This new era of franchise basketball has only just reached equilibrium.

It’s a lovely place to end the regular season. It’s not where they want to end the year.

“We want more out of these playoffs,” Johnson said on Thursday. “We want to play more basketball.”

The Mystics’ dramatic turnaround has put considerable focus on their youth. (They are, indeed, the youngest roster to qualify for the playoffs in the history of the WNBA, with six rookies and three sophomore players on the roster.) That has come with discussion about how they were not expected to be here, and how they are remarkably far ahead of schedule, and how they have an open window to contend in the future. All of that is true. But that is not quite the point for the Mystics.

As they see it: They are here now. The playoffs start on Sunday. They are ready to go.

“Coming into the season, we didn't have anything to lose, but we knew everything that we wanted to accomplish,” Mystics rookie forward Cotie McMahon said. “And we're here. We're accomplishing it all.”

Their win over the Sky on Thursday was shakier than it should have been. (An unusually lackadaisical fourth quarter meant they came uncomfortably close to blowing a 25-point lead.) But it was a win all the same, and it gave them the No. 5 seed, creating a first-round showdown with the No. 4 Dream.

In some ways, these rosters are intriguingly similar. No WNBA team gets more rebounds than Washington… but the one that comes closest is Atlanta. No WNBA team shoots more within five feet of the basket than Atlanta… but the one that comes closest is Washington. An intense paint matchup is a given. But there are several key stylistic differences here.

The Dream gain their defensive edge by forcing turnovers. (They lead the WNBA with 9.1 steals per game.) The Mystics have one of the best defenses in the league without forcing many turnovers. The Dream have more three-point shooting. The Mystics have more depth.

Back in June, when these teams first played each other this season, Atlanta dominated, 109-77. It was the worst loss of the year for Washington, and the ugliest, too: The ordinarily calm Johnson was ejected. But a young team can grow fast. The Mystics did not play a game like that again. They beat the Dream when they faced them in July and in August, a bit more cohesive, confident and calculated each time. They are eager to show just how much they have grown in September.

Mystics’ notes:

  • The team had a brief scare in the fourth quarter on Thursday when Shakira Austin hit the ground hard absorbing contact for a foul. After making her free throws—and receiving a standing ovation from the crowd—she went to the locker room and did not return. There was no official medical update immediately after the game. But Johnson said that he did not see any cause for great concern: “I’m expecting that she’ll be with us,” he said about her status for Game 1, noting that she had been smiling in the locker room.
  • Thursday night was the Mystics’ one and only game this season at Capital One Arena. (With the building undergoing renovations this summer, the team did not have the opportunity to host additional games downtown, as it often has in years past: Every previous home game this season was played at their standard home arena, CareFirst, in Southeast D.C.) And don’t count on that changing in the event of a deep playoff run. Cap One is booked with concerts, Wizards and Capitals games for the dates of nearly all potential future postseason games. Expect the playoff journey to run through CareFirst.

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: The Master Plan
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Sept. 25, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: Final plans for a new Commanders stadium, no verdict (yet) for Trayon White and the Mystics get ready for the playoffs.

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit: 7/10. Mainly bright but breezy. Still, it’s plenty comfortable with temperatures up a handful of degrees from yesterday. Full forecast from Capital Weather.

THE LATEST

A “whole new neighborhood” is coming to D.C.

Mayor Muriel Bowser submitted final plans for the new, $3.8 billion Commanders stadium and wider RFK campus to the D.C. Council on Thursday, informed by months of local outreach and thousands of public comments on a draft version of the plan published in June, The Washington Sun’s Michael Brice-Saddler reports.

Bidding for construction will begin in November and December, with stadium foundation work slated for the spring. The 65,000-seat stadium is expected to open in 2030, and will host 200 events a year.

The plans are far larger than just a stadium. The master plan promises to generate some $4 billion in tax revenue, create 30,000 construction jobs as well as 2,000 permanent positions, and build between 5,500 and 6,500 new homes — with at least 30% designated as affordable — as well as commercial spaces and a grocery store.

Controversially, to some in Ward 7 and beyond, the plans officially nix adding a second Metro stadium to the site. A summary document from the city’s Office of Planning notes that WMATA concluded the idea was infeasible due to “cost, engineering and timeline constraints.”

The transit authority maintains that an expansion of Stadium-Armory and a new rapid-transit bus line will be enough to ferry game-goers to and from the stadium, and Bowser said the bus — dubbed the Gold Line — will be ready for 2030.

“This is our obligation,” she said.


FROM THE COURTHOUSE

The jury deliberated for a second day without reaching a verdict in the bribery trial of D.C. Council member Trayon White, The Sun’s Jenny Gathright reports. Jurors asked the judge a question: Is it bribery if the defendant received money to perform an official act, but had no intention of fulfilling the agreement? The answer was no. Deliberations resume this morning.





FROM THE DISTRICT

Evictions in D.C. need to be speedier, about 60 landlords said this week while advocating for two housing bills, The Sun’s Zara Norman reports. One would make it easier to kick squatters out of short-term rentals, and the other would set a 60-day deadline for initial court hearings in lease violation cases. The changes are needed, landlords say, because tenant nonpayment and protracted court processes are pushing them to the brink, and sometimes out of business.

Tenant advocates warned that that could backfire, given how strained D.C.’s courts are already, and pointed to record numbers of evictions in 2025 as evidence that the system is working.

Janeese Lewis George’s listening session for Ward 3, held at Saint Sophia Greek Orthodox Cathedral, drew more than 500 RSVPs, The Sun’s Michael Brice-Saddler reports, which forced organizers to extend the event space outdoors.

“We had to move outside because so many people want to be engaged in local government,” the city’s likely next mayor told the crowd. Ward 3, D.C.’s whitest and wealthiest ward, is the only one she did not win in the June Democratic primary. “Be open to this experience,” she said to the attendees.

During the session, many residents voiced concerns regarding the state of the ward’s affordable-housing supply and the gaps between schools, among other issues. Acknowledging that she was not immediately familiar with everyone in the room, Lewis George said she plans to create an “accountability scorecard” for residents to hold her to her promises.

Three teens arrested in connection with a May brawl at a Chipotle in Navy Yard have entered into plea agreements. Two pleaded guilty to simple assault, while a third pleaded guilty to assault with a deadly weapon. The 16-year-old defendants are required to do community service, abide by “stay-away” orders and write apology letters to Chipotle staff, victims and witnesses. Charges for the teens have the potential to be dismissed, but they face incarceration until age 21 if they fail to comply with court orders. A fourth teen is scheduled for a court hearing next month.

D.C. Health collected only 10% of the standard medical forms required to enroll students in the District’s public and charter schools last fiscal year, At-Large council member and health committee chair Christina Henderson posted on X. At a public hearing Thursday, a school nurse of 10 years testified that she’d never been asked to submit the forms. Rachel Johnston, D.C. Charter School Alliance’s chief of staff, testified that she wasn’t sure whether D.C. Health could access the school portals that parents use to upload student health records.

DOGE pains: The local economy and employment landscape are still recovering from the effects of a massive reduction to the federal workforce that has slashed 50,000 positions in the D.C. region since early 2025, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports.





FROM VIRGINIA

Free doesn’t always mean free. Alexandria overspent by $3.7 million on public buses — which are free to riders — last year largely because of a spreadsheet error, The Washington Post reports.





FROM MARYLAND

What happens in Vegas doesn’t always stay in Vegas. A smaller version of the famed Sphere, a massive events venue built in Las Vegas in 2023, is coming to Prince George’s County. But local workers are pushing for a labor agreement before they give their support to the $1.4 billion project, The Sun’s Justice Covert writes.





METRO MOMENT


Landlord Jacques Chevalier provided some levity to an otherwise serious housing hearing yesterday, saying in his testimony:

“This is my hometown. I was born here — D.C. General. So is my wife,” he said. “So is my side piece.”

He added: “That part was a joke, y’all. My wife’s gonna kill me.”





SPORTS

The Mystics closed out the regular season with a big win over the Chicago Sky. In a game where they never trailed and led by as many as 25, they locked in the No. 5 seed in the WNBA playoffs, which start on Sunday. It’s been a remarkable stretch run for the youngest team in the league, winning seven of their last eight. Their first-round playoff opponent will be the No. 4 seed Atlanta Dream.

Training camp started last week for the Capitals. It’s already nearly over. Such is life now in the NHL, where a new collective bargaining agreement has brought a new schedule, with a shorter training camp and shorter preseason. For a team like the Capitals, who made several big acquisitions over the summer, that leaves a brief window to integrate new talent and make tough roster calls. “It’s more difficult, no doubt,” Capitals coach Spencer Carbery said.

What to Watch Today:

MLB: Nationals vs. Mets, 6:45 p.m.

entries.title: The Washington Sun: Panic Week
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Felt like an inflection point this week. Who got the coveted state dinner ticket. The district to watch this November. A new poll shows a real Senate race in Nebraska. And: Check out our No. 1 story. 





THE LATEST

This was not the week Republicans were looking for. Something feels different about the midterms at the end of this week than at the start. It’s like everyone suddenly got on the same page.

“I don’t want to say the bottom is falling out yet, but I feel like we are in this place, and the realization is setting in, that some tough decisions will need to be made,” a Republican consultant told our Elena Schneider. “You can’t get around the fact that Democrats have the advantage on the economy, on gas prices. There’s no choice in this election. It’s a referendum on Trump.”

We asked our colleagues covering the midterms for The Washington Sun what this week meant for November.

Our Alex Roarty pointed out that it’s not as if the reality of the political situation changed all that much — polls this week weren’t much worse than they had been in past months — but Republican candidates seemed to realize all at once that they might be stuck with a difficult climate all the way through November. “Republicans say there’s still time for their ads to blunt Democratic momentum but acknowledge that the window to do so shrinks every day,” he writes.

Donald Trump made the election to be about him in Dallas, the idea being that rallying around the president would be helpful for Republicans. But all over the battleground map, they’re trying to get distance from him. Candidates we never imagined wanting space from the president are out there being critical — the proto-MAGA Paul LePage is knocking the White House’s immigration enforcement efforts?? Yikes.

The panicked post on X by MAGA-aligned radio host Steve Deace on Wednesday — sure to go down as one of the all-time election freakouts — summarizes the widening realization. (“GOP Is BLOWING IT” was the title of his Thursday podcast, in case people hadn’t picked up what he was putting down on X.)

Articulating issues near and dear to the electorate in general has proven challenging for Republicans this week. Our Igor Bobic reports that the Senate is sticking around the Capitol to stay hard at work on … a college sports bill. Barring something really surprising happening, there will be no new affordability-focused legislation before Election Day. Trump, meanwhile, has been tied up all week with foreign leaders. Can’t be helped, the calendar is the calendar. But also: pretty terrible timing.

There’s a lot of time on the clock still, and Republicans are outspending Democrats thanks to MAGA Inc.’s endless money spigot. The ads “still need some time to sink in for voters,” goes the thinking among some Republicans, according to Alex. The Democratic brand is bad, they note, and Republicans bet working-class voters will tune in late and are more up for grabs than the polls indicate. Just chill out a little, they suggested this week. Stick with the program.

But this is the week where any remaining chill was officially retired. The Sun’s Oriana González was chatting with one Republican House member about the idea the House might get called back from recess to work on some kind of affordability bill. The notion is “tough” to imagine, the lawmaker said — everyone is scared to leave the campaign trail now. The “environment is way worse than many probably thought.”

FROM THE WHITE HOUSE


State dinner highlights: Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping in the East Room last night, with the two leaders toasting each other over glasses of Schramsberg Blanc de Noir, the same wine served during Richard Nixon’s famous 1972 “Toast to Peace” in Beijing, The Sun’s Gavin J. Quinton and Jasmine Wright report.

The lengthy guest list included tech billionaires like Mark Zuckerberg, Sam Altman and Elon Musk. Most reporters were not welcomed into the East Room for the meal, with the exception of a group of Fox News personalities, including Laura Ingraham, Bret Baier and Jesse Watters.

Classifying the emerging tech: The federal government classifies water systems, emergency services and energy infrastructure as critical, so what about AI? Some researchers of the technology are discussing whether it should be defined as “critical infrastructure,” a move that would allow coordination with federal agencies on safety, The Sun’s Mara Hoplamazian reports. The discussion has reached the Trump administration, which is keen on AI these days.

More: Chinese Press Corps Scuffles With U.S. Media and Secret Service • Mark Carney Says He Has Prepared for the Possibility of a U.S. Invasion • Trump Administration Asks SCOTUS to Let It Restart Its Third-Country Deportation Push

FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL


Watch Virginia’s 1st District, advises The Sun’s Paul Kane. Republican Rep. Rob Wittman is a lawmaker from the old era when voters often told pollsters they disliked Congress but liked their own representative, Paul writes. But those days might be finished. Wittman is in a real race, and a smart one to tune into — since Virginia finishes its ballot counting quicker than most states on Election Day, how this seat goes could show how the nation is going.

First on The Sun: Internal polling shows a real Senate race in Nebraska. Independent Dan Osborn is up by 1 percentage point against Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts, 47-46, in the survey. The internal poll, conducted by a pro-Osborn super PAC and obtained first by The Sun’s Elena Schneider, found independent voters backing Osborn by a 45-percentage-point edge. Trump is also underwater, with just 44% approving of his job performance to 49% who did not.

More: Tom Tiffany’s Campaign Bars a Reporter From Entering Campaign Event

FROM THE HILL


Little help on the legislative front: Locked in a tough reelection race, Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) would love to get her bill lowering the cost of insulin through the Senate and head home to campaign on helping Americans grappling with higher costs of living. “It’s completely bipartisan and it would make a big difference to a lot of people,” Collins told The Sun’s Avani Kalra. Alas, that bill and many others aren’t on the final agenda right now for the upper chamber in the days before it adjourns before the midterms.

“It should have been brought up a long time before now,” Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana) said of the insulin bill. Sen. Jim Justice (R-West Virginia) backs the bill and wants it passed. But, he adds, “everybody here is running to get home.”

NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

It’s the only way to go: Flanked by two portraits of long-gone, deceased speakers, these House bathrooms are the answer to nature’s call — and reporters hoping for a quote. Many an impromptu press conference develops near this unhallowed spot. The Sun’s Emily Kennard takes us outside the restrooms just off the House floor. “Duly elected members of Congress are constitutionally required to be human, and all humans are biologically required to pee,” Emily writes in what is likely the best sentence of her career.

And fair warning: One House Democrat, granted anonymity to speak candidly about his colleagues’ hygiene, told The Sun that many male members who use the restroom by the chamber — generally, like men using any bathroom — don’t wash their hands.

“I wouldn’t shake hands with anyone that comes out of the bathroom,” the lawmaker said.

entries.title: Inside the Freakout Over AI Testing in Government Websites
entries.summary: A rush of AI into government web development is worrying tech workers over accessibility.
entries.content:
Over the course of the last week and a half, two government technology officials — one an artificial intelligence engineer and the second a former DOGE affiliate — proposed a flurry of changes to the code that underpins at least 600 government websites.

A government contractor posted a plea for “some communication please” from the two officials.

Artificial intelligence “appears to be the driver,” the contractor wrote last week on the federal web design system’s GitHub page — a developer platform used to share and manage code. “It’s scaring” the federal agencies who use the web design system to build their own sites, the contractor wrote.

“An accessibility proven design system,” they continued, “seems to be taking a backseat to the AI push.”

The official communication that followed only deepened fears about the extent of the Trump administration's use of AI for government services. Ryan Parker, the AI engineer from the Treasury Department who is newly in charge of the government’s web design system, responded to the plea by saying he plans to fully automate accessibility testing on the government’s web design systems.

In other words, the Trump administration wants AI to conduct the tests that ensure that blind people and those with other disabilities can access the government websites that Americans use to sign up for benefits or find other critical information.

The outcry was immediate. The government’s own web page on Section 508, the legal requirement for government technology to be accessible, says that manual testing is necessary because some accessibility standards are “highly context-dependent and require human judgment to determine conformance.”

“No one’s been able to” automate accessibility testing, including large accessibility companies, one government technology employee told The Washington Sun. Changes made with “AI and the confidence of a coked-up teenager” could make the system — and websites that rely on it — less accessible, they said.

The idea is “dangerous,” said another government technology employee.

Both employees requested anonymity for fear of retribution. But backlash was apparent on the government GitHub page, where commenters raised concerns about removing human-run testing. In response, Parker and the former DOGE affiliate, Treasury Department Chief Information Officer Sam Corcos, appeared to be updating posts in real time and deleting comments that raised concerns.

Parker has edited his intentions for AI-powered accessibility several times, changing it from a goal to “automate the full range of accessibility tests needed” for the system to “automate as much accessibility testing as possible.” He also added — and removed — references to falling back on human testing as needed.

In another instance, Parker wrote: "We do not yet know whether every assessment can be automated reliably; demonstrating that reliability is part of the work."

Laura Gerhardt, a civic technologist and engineer who previously implemented the web design system at several agencies, left comments on the system’s GitHub detailing concerns about its overhaul apparently being led by a single engineer.

Corcos responded with a single word — “wrong” — at 4:32 a.m. Wednesday, according to screenshots viewed by The Sun. Since then, Gerhardt’s comments have been deleted and her ability to make further ones has been blocked, Gerhardt told The Sun.

Amanda Kelly, a former General Services Administration employee, also left a comment asking why other notes were being deleted. Those comments, too, were deleted, she confirmed to The Sun.

“The U.S. Web Design System is responsibly integrating AI tools, human review, and community input to improve accessibility,” a GSA spokesperson told The Sun. “Incorporating AI will result in identifying barriers earlier, expanding testing coverage, and improving accessibility while we validate reliability.”

President Donald Trump has made reshaping the way government websites look a priority; last year, he ordered his new National Design Studio — staffed by many prominent former DOGE associates — to overhaul the U.S. Web Design System. Whether the National Design Studio is involved currently is unclear. But the head of that design team has promised to overhaul the government’s entire online presence.

Many of those early efforts of the design studio have run into accessibility issues, as The Washington Sun has previously reported.

For over a decade, the General Services Administration has maintained the U.S. Web Design System. In recent weeks, that responsibility has been shifted from a small team at GSA and open-source contributors to two people: Corcos and Parker.

Corcos was installed in several roles at GSA last month. Since then, the sole full-time federal employee tasked with maintaining the design system was put on administrative leave. Open-source contributors — added after the main contract for the system was cut earlier this year — have been booted.

Matt Henry, who used to work on the system at GSA until last fall, is now encouraging those who use the system to use the “pre-slop” version archived before all these changes were made.

Now, the prospect of AI taking over accessibility testing is magnifying those worries.

Automated tools can’t test if a person can understand and use a website, digital accessibility expert Nicolas Steenhout wrote in a LinkedIn blog about the idea. The tools can technically run a screen reader — software that helps blind people use websites by reading the text on them out loud or offering a braille display— but they can’t see if those programs work for real people.

“I have never seen an automated testing tool that can capture the full range of accessibility issues,” said Beth DeConinck, an accessibility specialist who’s been in the field for a decade and previously worked as a government contractor.

Although she uses automated tools, most of her work is manual, DeConinck said, and she frequently uses the federal design system as a gut check for her work at a private company.

“This is a valuable resource for everybody, and I would hate for it to be ruined,” she said.

entries.title: The Best Place to Catch a Lawmaker? Where They Pee.
entries.summary: The facilities next to the lavish antechamber off the House floor are where many senior lawmakers make frequent stops.
entries.content:
Men in suits dutifully guard a door. They can’t go in behind their boss — the facility behind the door is too covert, the activities within too clandestine, maybe classified. Reporters huddle before the suits, phones at the ready, waiting for someone to emerge.

Then it happens: Speaker Mike Johnson is done in the restroom. The door swings open. His guards surround him, and reporters race along, putting a quick damper on the speaker’s physical relief.

Duly elected members of Congress are constitutionally required to be human, and all humans are biologically required to pee. On voting days, a member who chooses to do so in the nearest suitable facility puts themselves in the path of the horde of people who desperately want information from them.

Aside from the Republican cloakroom — which provides lawmakers with cheap hot dogs and grilled cheeses — the members-only bathrooms off the House floor, adjacent to the lavish Speaker’s Lobby, are some of the only places near the floor where lawmakers are out of view from the Hill’s many nosy reporters (though The Washington Sun once witnessed Fox News anchor Sean Hannity make a brief stop inside).

The air of exclusivity hovers over the facilities. Outside the bathroom doors, flanked by two portraits of long-gone, deceased speakers, a crystal chandelier hangs with chains of beads that stay busy catching and reflecting light. Like the rest of the halls surrounding the House floor, the ceilings are covered with ornate neoclassical details. And, on voting days, just as dependable as the chandelier hanging are the reporters leaning against the adjacent stairwell’s marble railing.

Those doors have seen many impromptu press conferences take place right outside. Members say inside, the restrooms are entirely normal, with minimal issues (except in April, when one toilet in the men’s restroom profusely leaked into the hallway, and water seeped through the floor onto the one below).

Still, members know that running off the floor to use the restroom during a long vote series means they’ll inevitably have to cross the strategic chokepoint essential to Hill reporting.

When Democratic black sheep Rep. Jared Golden of Maine — notorious for avoiding the press during votes — helped Republicans pass a rule on Sept. 1, a Washington Sun reporter saw him enter the restroom, waited for his exit and asked whether he informed leadership of his apostasy beforehand (the answer was a resounding “no”).

Some members said they’re resigned to the unavoidable reality of facing the bathroom stakeout. “It’s a fait accompli. It’s a part of life,” said Rep. Jake Ellzey (R-Texas), who said he doesn’t get mobbed enough to mind.

“You guys have the right to hang out anywhere you want to, and it just so happens that’s where that thing is,” Ellzey added.

Between members, the hallway has a cordial culture. When members traverse the hallway and spot their buddies leaving the bathroom, they can be seen offering handshakes, back pats and fist bumps. Sometimes, like young women at a bar, they exit the room together in couples or groups, laughing to themselves about whatever they were discussing inside.

One House Democrat, granted anonymity to speak candidly about his colleagues' hygiene, told The Sun that many male members who use the restroom by the chamber — generally, like men using any bathroom — don't wash their hands.

"I wouldn't shake hands with anyone that comes out of the bathroom," the lawmaker said.

Besides worrying Congress’ attending physician, the alleged lack of hand-washing might cause unease among leadership in both parties, given their concerns about member sickness and attendance, since Republicans have a slim majority this Congress.

Rep. Mike Kennedy (R-Utah), a freshman, admitted it’s a smart place for reporters to stand.

“If you’re looking at the physiologic necessity of having to go to the toilet at some point, you’ll capture most people around the floor if you sit out there,” said Kennedy, a family physician.

That didn’t make it any less bizarre for him when he started his job at the Hill, though: “It’s weird. There’s a bunch of ladies hanging out by the men’s bathroom,” Kennedy added, laughing.

Freshman Rep. Mike Haridopolos (R-Florida) said it was a “new experience” for him, since press wasn’t allowed around the restrooms in the Florida state Senate, where he worked before. “I hope we don’t stink up your place,” he said. (The hallway is only occasionally stinky.)

But other lawmakers are now pushing to bar reporters from that hallway altogether. Rep. Mark Alford (R-Missouri) said “there’s a movement underway” to keep the press out of the Speaker’s Lobby hallway next Congress.

Even when lawmakers escape to their members-only bathrooms, though, it’s not like any groundbreaking bipartisan compromises get worked out at the sinks.

“You have Republicans and Democrats in there, so it sort of constrains a lot of talk,” said Rep. Don Bacon (R-Nebraska), who’s retiring from Congress. Besides, as Rep. Dan Meuser (R-Pennsylvania) pointed out, the acoustics of the bathroom don’t seem suitable for low-key legislative dealmaking — “You have so many other places, the cloakroom, the floor. Think about it: It echoes in there; you really can’t whisper.”

The men’s room used to have one convenient luxury, according to retiring Rep. Steve Cohen (D-Tennessee), who said as recently as around 10 years ago, the bathroom had a “nice fellow” who would shine members’ shoes for tips between votes.

While little politicking seems to go on behind the doors, bathrooms have been at the center of a major political fight this Congress. After the chamber was set to receive its first transgender member in November 2024, Rep. Sarah McBride (D-Delaware), House leadership acted to ensure that she would be banned from using the women’s restroom. And the same month McBride took office, Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colorado) reportedly complained to House security about “a guy” in the members-only women’s restroom, according to reporter Billy House. (She later admitted she was mistaken.)

The women’s restroom next to the House floor is also a remarkably recent addition: It was only added in 2011, nearly 100 years after the first-ever woman served in Congress. Before, women members had to run through Statuary Hall to relieve themselves.

The proximity of the bathrooms has led to some confusion, though.

“A lady congressman that was a freshman happened to walk into the wrong one, thinking that it was the women’s room and realized somewhat quickly, let’s just say, that the infrastructure was not appropriate for the ladies’ restroom,” Rep. Russ Fulcher (R-Idaho) said.

The particular demographic makeup of the Republican House majority can guide where reporters go when they’re looking for information from the people who, at least for now, hold the most power. Standing next to the men’s restroom makes sense: Only 30 of the GOP’s voting members are women, and only one is a chair of a major committee, according to the House Republicans’ website.

The average age of the 21 male Republican chairs is 62, when Americans can begin receiving Social Security retirement benefits. Aging is known to make bladders stiffer and make their muscles weaker, meaning older people tend to have to pee more.

Appropriations Chair Tom Cole, 77, is a case in point. While Cole’s office serves as another nearby hideout for Republicans, especially those who partake in cigar smoking, it doesn’t have its own bathroom. Oklahomans who want to hear from their most powerful congressman, or reporters who need updates on appropriations bills or negotiations, depend on his deliberate treks back and forth between the floor, the bathroom and his office for a chance to catch him.

Whether lawmakers are longtime veterans of the chamber, or fresh-faced newly elected members, the architectural reality of the bathrooms seems widely understood: There’s only one entrance, and it’s the same as the exit.

“If we go in there, we gotta come out. So I mean, it works,” said Rep. Jimmy Patronis (R-Florida), a freshman.

And Patronis, looking on the bright side of risking being confronted every time he exits the restroom as part of his daily life at work, had the highest of compliments to share about it.

“I’m in the restaurant business. Clean bathrooms are important. And so for me to notice, it means they’re doing the right thing,” he added. “[The Capitol’s bathrooms] are always clean. This one here is. Now, nothing special about it. I don’t know what the ladies’ rooms look like.”

entries.title: The Surprising District That Could Determine the House Majority
entries.summary: All eyes turn to… Virginia?
entries.content:
WILLIAMSBURG, Va. — Shannon Taylor’s plan to defeat Republican Rep. Rob Wittman, an almost 20-year incumbent, is to turn his strength into a weakness.

She’s taking the fact that Wittman has served his Northern Neck region for decades — from a town council victory in 1986 to state government, then Congress two decades later — and using it against him.Washington has changed him, she says.

“I hear the stories, and the way I categorize it is: He's lost his way, he was somebody that people thought they could count on over 20 years ago, and they can't count on him now,” Taylor told The Washington Sun.

Thirteen members of Congress lost their primaries this summer — seven Democrats and six Republicans — and Taylor is hoping an anti-incumbent summer turns into an anti-incumbent fall.

What happens in the commonwealth will also give a window into what happens everywhere: Since Virginia finishes its ballot counting quicker than most states on Election Day, early calls in two House races that stretch south and east from Richmond and across the Chesapeake Bay will be key for determining the House majority.

In Virginia’s 2nd Congressional District, anchored around Virginia Beach, Republican Rep. Jen Kiggans is in a rematch with her 2022 opponent, Elaine Luria, who held the seat from 2019 into 2023.

It’s a classic swing district: Republicans have won it five times and Democrats three times since 2008. Adding up vote totals for each party in the last four contests, Democrats received 660,000 votes in the 2nd District while Republican candidates received 659,000.

A Kiggans victory would suggest Republicans could weather the storm in 21 tossup races, as rated by the Cook Political Report.

But a Democratic victory in the 1st District would signal that a blue wave would rise high enough to swamp once safe incumbents like Wittman, who has won every reelection contest by double digit margins.

Taylor, 58, a county prosecutor in Richmond’s suburbs, portrays herself as a tough-on-crime Democrat. She might remind some voters of Gov. Abigail Spanberger, who flipped a longtime Republican seat outside Richmond in 2018 and went on to a blowout victory in last year’s gubernatorial race.

Taylor is running on an anti-corruption message that raps Wittman for years of trading stocks in his personal portfolio despite voting for a ban on such trades. She also supports a 12-year limit on terms in the House and Senate and a lifetime prohibition on former members becoming lobbyists.

“Put your money where your mouth is, right? If I come up with these anti-corruption proposals, they are proposals that I'm going to follow,” she said after touring a local community health clinic.

Wittman, 67, is a head-down lawmaker who believes he has the right experience. He focuses heavily on the House Armed Services Committee and defense-related projects he has delivered for his military-centric district. If he wins, he could become the top Republican on the coveted committee next year.

“Experience matters,” he told a local TV station in a profile that ran this month.

One of his first ads — he had four times as much campaign money to spend in the final four months of the race — literally mapped out the drive he takes to Washington rather than renting an apartment on Capitol Hill.

“I never forgot who I represent because I never left,” he said.

This district was actually ranked as the absolute political median out of 435 House seats, according to a University of Virginia analysis. It will serve as a political science experiment about whether no-frills incumbents can still win in an era where many lawmakers run to social media and ideological cable news for political adrenaline hits.

Wittman is a lawmaker from the old era when voters often told pollsters they disliked Congress but liked their own representative.

Those days might be finished.

Today’s Congress is reviled across the political spectrum. President Donald Trump’s own disapproval among voters — some polls show close to two-thirds of voters opposed to his job performance — looks rosy when compared to the 80 to 85% of voters who have disapproved of Congress for the past year, according to Gallup’s monthly poll.

An unpopular president overseeing an unpopular war abroad and soaring gas prices at home, mixed in with a toxic brand for Congress, opened the doors for Democrats to move beyond just the traditional battlegrounds like Virginia’s 2nd District.

Wittman’s district has favored Trump all three times he appeared on the presidential ballot. Yet his margin has shrunk from a robust 14-point win here in 2016 to less than 5 percentage points in 2024.

The growing Richmond suburbs now account for more than 40% of the votes, and Spanberger broke through and won this district in her gubernatorial race by more than 2 points.

Democratic Sen. Mark Warner is coasting to a reelection victory over a little-known challenger, giving him a chance to run up his vote tally in rural areas that he still covets as other Virginia Democrats focus heavily on urban areas.

That leaves down-ballot Republicans like Wittman without any cover from above.

Wittman knows his district has changed and he’s prepared for this race like never before. By June 30 he had raised more than $4 million, twice as much as he raised for the entire 2022 campaign.

Republicans point to the bounce-back in the spring when the Democratic-dominated state legislature put a referendum before voters to gerrymander the congressional lines: Conservatives here turned out and the “no” side won by 10 points, even as the ballot won a narrow victory statewide.

That referendum became national news as the Democratic response to Republican-led states like Texas and Ohio drawing new lines to try to fortify the majority for House Speaker Mike Johnson (Louisiana).

But after the Virginia Supreme Court struck down the referendum, after its narrow passage, the spotlight shifted to other states. It’s now shifting back to the commonwealth.

Taylor, who narrowly lost a bid for the Democratic nomination for state attorney general last year, rarely mentions the president’s name on the stump. She’s aware that she needs to win over voters who have supported the president at least once, if not more.

“We talk about Rob Wittman. He's the person that is trying to be rehired for his job, and I'm the one who's highlighting why he needs to be fired from his job,” she told The Sun.

Independent partisan groups have flooded the district, which is split between the Richmond and Norfolk media markets, with ads on local TV.

By early August, road signs lined many of the highways that boiled each party’s message down to its most basic form:

“No on Wittman, we can’t afford him.”

“Vote common sense, vote Republican.”

Taylor and her allies have pinned higher prices on Republicans and policy decisions related to tariffs and the Iran war. While touring the Olde Towne Medical & Dental Center, she peppered the staff with questions about drops in patients using Medicaid given Republican cuts to the healthcare program to finance permanent tax cuts.

In August, 109 fewer patients used Medicaid and 111 more showed up without any insurance, according to Aaron Thompson, the center’s CEO.

“It’s almost like we’re going back in time,” he told Taylor.

Wittman has tapped into the type of culture wars that Trump used so successfully in his presidential bids, highlighting cases where Taylor sought lesser jail time for criminals.

“She lets the worst criminals out of jail early,” he said in one ad, as local sheriffs stand behind him.

Taylor’s team has reams of data points showing how crime has gone down in Henrico County, but she also often points to her prosecution of a prominent Democratic state legislator for sexual misconduct with minors.

She says she expects to stand up to the far-left wing of the House Democratic caucus, which will be populated next year by several new members who espouse socialist views.

Ultimately, the race could turn on whether Taylor can successfully turn Wittman’s tenure against him.

Wittman told his local TV station that voters still value someone with a four-decade record of serving local, county, state and federal government.

“That experience has taught me that good public policy is not about how something looks on paper. It is about whether it actually works for the people and communities,” he said.

Taylor reiterated her pledge to support term limits because voters “hate what they see both parties doing.”

“If we put a restriction on how long someone can actually serve, maybe they will focus on the job that they're supposed to be doing,” she said.

entries.title: D.C. Landlords Push the Council to Allow Speedier Evictions
entries.summary: Thursday’s council hearing featured a clash over how to balance renter protections with what landlords describe as an economic “death spiral.”
entries.content:
Last September, the D.C. Council passed a bill that landlords called a “win” — one they hoped would restore eviction speeds back to pre-pandemic levels.

Just a year later, around 60 of them came back to say the council needs to go farther to protect housing providers from becoming insolvent and to continue to attract investment in the city.

“It did very little to impact the crisis,” Dean Hunter, the CEO of D.C.’s Small Multifamily Owners Association, now says of last year’s bill. “Our economic vacancy is at record levels, couple that with the fact that possession cases are taking 18 months to two years. You see the harm. A landlord's bills are still due, the mortgage is still due. We've devastated the industry.”

That bill — The RENTAL, or “Rebalancing Expectations for Neighbors, Tenants and Landlords,” Act — made it easier to secure an initial eviction hearing more quickly and reduced the initial notice period from 30 to 10 days.

D.C. landlords testified this week advocating for two separate bills that would speed things up further. The Housing Investment Protection Act, heard by the housing committee on Thursday, would introduce a mandatory 60-day initial hearing period on lease violation cases. Another, heard by the judiciary and public safety committee on Wednesday, would make it easier to evict squatters from short-term housing. Landlords pushed for that to be expanded to include long-term housing, too.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

“I expect this to be a battle, and we’re going to win,” Hunter told The Washington Sun. “We got [the RENTAL Act] done, and we're going to get this done.”

‘This is What a Death Spiral Looks Like’

During the COVID-19 pandemic, courts paused eviction cases if the tenant had submitted an application for emergency rental assistance. Landlords say that created a backlog of cases, and while those played out, they didn’t receive the rental money they rely on to pay their mortgage, utility bills or make basic repairs.

“Landlords go without important revenue that helps them send their kids to college, make mortgage payments or, in my case, pay for the round-the-clock home health aides to care for their elderly parents,” local landlord Kelly Brown testified at Thursday’s hearing.

Hunter surveyed 621 of his member landlords, finding that 70% of respondents reported that completed possession cases took at least a year, during which time very few tenants made regular rent payments.

For smaller landlords owning 10 or fewer units — who, Hunter asserts, make up 80% of property owners in the District — it’s left them holding the bag and selling their properties short of their value.

“We're seeing losses to owners unlike anything we've seen before. My own family has invested in real estate for over 50 years in D.C., and we've stopped investing in multifamily properties,” testified Tim Dudley, an investor and property manager with Dudley Pro Realty.

A quicker initial hearing period would limit those losses, owners testified. It could also help tenants from falling so far behind in payments that they can’t hope to make their balance up, Hunter said.

“Many properties are falling further into disrepair as both financial conditions deteriorate and property management firms continue to exit the market,” testified Patrick McAnaney, development director of the Somerset Development Company. “Mission-oriented housing providers are selling off their properties to stay afloat. This is what a death spiral looks like.”

‘Evictions Should Be Rare and Fair’

But tenant advocates don’t think speeding up the eviction process will pull landlords out of that spiral. They argue that, a year out, the full effects of the RENTAL Act still haven’t been felt and that D.C.’s court system is so overburdened that adding to its load may slow down the eviction process even further.

“Setting deadlines for the court, while at the same time piling on new processes and opening the door to a flood of eviction filings, is not realistic in practice and certainly would not make things move faster,” testified Elena Bowers, the managing attorney of Legal Aid D.C.’s housing law unit.

Council member Brooke Pinto, who chairs the judiciary committee, emphasized that point in Thursday’s housing committee hearing.

“I want to note how frustrating it has been to see a Congress hold flat the funding for our courts over the last several years, even as we've seen a demand grow, and last year passed a budget that will lead to a $20 million reduction in our courts,” she said.

Attorneys and tenant advocates urged the council to steer away from passing another sweeping package of reforms and instead look to prevent eviction cases from being filed in the first place.

“Evictions should be rare and fair,” testified Maya Brennan, chief housing officer of the Coalition for Nonprofit Housing and Economic Development. “The changes we've seen over the past year appear to move us in the right direction. Cases are being heard, rulings are being made, protective orders are largely working. The court is working hard to address the backlog and to do so without returning to the days of no-show default judgments against tenants.”

Both the squatters bill and the Housing Investment Protection Act only received their first hearings, but the housing committee’s chair, Robert White, an at-large council member and D.C.’s Democratic nominee for congressional delegate, clearly signaled his position from the outset.

“While timelines may be slower than in years past, and we do have eviction issues, the District is completing evictions at a historically high level,” White said at Thursday’s hearing.

In the 2025 fiscal year, 2,614 evictions were completed, White said, compared to just 1,460 in 2016. The Senate, he added, confirmed six new D.C. Superior Court judges in August to fill long-standing vacancies. The idea that the District is not evicting residents for nonpayment of rent is a “false narrative,” White said.

Hunter called White a “tenant advocate.” He expects Pinto’s squatter bill to pass without too much struggle, but insists that landlords will push the Housing Investment Protection Act over the mountain, too.

“Let me be clear,” he said. “I will not hesitate to use every means at our disposal, including going to Congress and, if necessary, the Trump administration.”

entries.title: D.C.’s Workforce Is Still Recovering From Massive Federal Job Cuts
entries.summary: The effects of government layoffs can still be felt in the local economy, according to a new report.
entries.content:
The local workforce is still reeling from the effects of federal government cuts and job loss, which have devastated the capital since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term.

A new report from the D.C. Policy Center, commissioned by the D.C. Chamber of Commerce, paints a picture of a struggling city trying to claw its way back from devastating layoffs made in the name of government efficiency. In a region with the highest concentration of federal workers in the country, high unemployment rates are seeping into many aspects of the local economy, making it worse for wear.

“For more than two decades, the city benefited from a growth model driven by federal expansion, population growth, rising commercial real estate values, and an influx of highly educated workers,” the report said. “That growth model is now under pressure.”

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Substantial reductions within the federal sector have compounded the already struggling job market. The number of total jobs in the city is lower now than before the COVID-19 pandemic, with 86,900 less jobs in May 2026 than in February 2020. The number of unemployed D.C. residents increased by 8% in that same time frame, according to the 2026 State of Business report released Thursday.

Federal government employment within the District is down 14.6% as of May 2026 compared to January 2025. That number only accounts for civil servants — not federal contractors, intelligence agency employees or non-active-duty military — so the real impact is likely larger. That’s a big hit for a city where federal jobs make up a quarter of the workforce. In that same time period, the District’s overall unemployment rate increased by 4.4%.

Metrics that predict the future don’t look promising, either. The number of job openings is declining, as is the number of people leaving jobs voluntarily, which suggests less confidence that better opportunities are open in the District. Even though there are plenty of people looking for work, the job opportunities are not meeting the demand.

There are glimmers of hope for D.C.’s economic future, as a report released last week by real estate firm CBRE found that the U.S. government had added 1,400 jobs to the D.C. region between May and July, likely an indicator that the government originally made too many rollbacks. While that number is moving in the right direction, it does little to offset the estimated 50,000 federal jobs cut since early 2025.

entries.title: How ‘Critical’ Is AI?
entries.summary: The growing debate around whether to declare AI “critical infrastructure” has made it to the Trump administration.
entries.content:
Artificial intelligence now underpins major parts of the U.S. economy, from how financial institutions forecast and trade to how the energy industry plans and secures the power grid.

But should AI be considered “critical infrastructure” in the eyes of the federal government? Should it be legally designated in the same way as energy infrastructure, water systems and emergency services — sectors so important to U.S. society that disruptions could be disastrous?

The question is percolating among AI researchers — a community that has become increasingly influential as the fast-moving technology prompts novel safety questions — and even made its way to the acting director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which oversees such designations.

As lawmakers grapple with doomsday warnings about AI and the federal government incorporates the technology into everything from military operations to air traffic control, some of these researchers see the potential for the idea to make it to the White House.

“As this technology becomes more pervasive and more important to everyday U.S. lives, and it becomes an increasing target for threat actors, there really needs to be front-end resilience built in,” said Jess Maksimov, one such researcher, a policy analyst for Americans for Responsible Innovation. “Disruptions can really be cascading and debilitating.”

Maskimov’s white paper, written with co-researcher Terrence Kelly, is among several recommendations making the rounds in Washington on ways to secure AI infrastructure. Another report, from the American Security Project and researchers at Columbia University, recommended designating data centers as a critical infrastructure sector, as well as increasing funding and personnel for CISA, which manages coordination around those sectors.

At a June conference, CISA acting director Nick Andersen was asked whether he considered AI to be “critical infrastructure.” Initially, Andersen said no.

“I think the things that go into it and make it work are probably critical infrastructure,” he said, “which maybe is a distinction without a difference.”

But he acknowledged that a sector designation could be possible. And at least, he said, formal coordination among frontier AI labs and the federal government will increase, in an attempt to answer three defining questions: “How do we secure from adversarial AI, how do we secure our AI, and how do we use AI to help secure ourselves?”

In a statement to The Washington Sun, Andersen said his agency recognizes the transformative power of AI, but he didn’t comment on whether he supported a sector designation.

“We are committed to promoting the secure use of AI while ensuring that innovation—crucial to America’s global competitiveness—is not hindered. We actively collaborate with our partners on shared priorities, staying informed about the latest advancements in AI and exploring how these technologies can strengthen the nation’s defenses against cyber threats,” he said.

Currently, the federal government has designated 16 sectors as critical infrastructure, including banks, dams and military supply chains.

Giving AI this designation would create a way for the industry to coordinate with federal agencies on security risks. It could also subject AI companies to reporting requirements for major cyberattacks. Under the direction of Congress, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency could also establish security standards for AI infrastructure.

The idea has gathered interest in both conservative and liberal circles, despite being largely absent from AI policy conversations in the White House or on the Hill.

Chris Krebs, who led CISA under the first Trump administration, said as digital systems have become a core part of modern conflict and run-of-the-mill crime, AI is enhancing threats. A “critical infrastructure” designation could help create a forum for regular conversations between AI companies and different parts of the federal government, like the Energy or Commerce departments.

A designation could streamline the way the industry shares information with federal officials and allow for AI companies to work together on safety standards without concerns about market manipulation or price fixing.

Krebs noted that under the Trump administration, the Department of Homeland Security has made changes to the framework for partnerships, and it remains to be seen what impacts that will have.

“Companies have been doing this stuff for a very long time, and things have, on the whole, gotten better as a result of these sorts of collaborations,” Krebs said. “I would rather have a mechanism like this than nothing at all, and possibly even [more than] really aggressive regulation.”

But there are a lot of details to work out. Among cybersecurity experts, it brings up questions around what counts as AI infrastructure, what powers CISA could exercise over the industry, and whether the embattled agency has capacity to take on a new sector.

The agency lost a third of its workforce after layoffs, buyouts, early retirement and reassignments of personnel to ICE and Customs and Border Protection.

Frank Cilluffo, director of the McCrary Institute for Cyber and Critical Infrastructure Security at Auburn University, said AI is “without a doubt” critical. But he said he was worried that a designation could function like a checkbox, letting lawmakers and federal officials off the hook for other kinds of safeguards. And, he said, he’d want to understand exactly what kinds of potential regulation the move would entail.

“A designation of critical infrastructure doesn’t have to lead to a regulatory approach, but that is the natural gravitation that some of the agencies would go to,” he said.

That potential for additional layers of red tape has sparked skepticism.

“I think it sounds nice to do, but I also think it doesn’t bring a whole lot of real safety and security. It brings a lot more bureaucratic ordination,” said Mark Dalton, a policy director at the center-right R Street Institute. “I don’t think actual tangible security benefits arise from that.”

There may be too many sectors already, he argued. “If 16 things are critical, then which one of those is critical?” he said.

President Donald Trump has called fears around AI safety a “hoax.” Even so, his administration recently proposed a shared notification system that would allow China and the United States to alert one another to AI incidents that threaten national security.

Proponents of making AI “critical infrastructure” say it won’t necessarily lead to more regulations.

“It’s a partnership, really,” Maksimov said. The public sector provides insight, resources and coordination on national security concerns, but “the onus is mostly on industry to make sure that their specific technologies are secure.”

No new critical infrastructure sectors have been designated since 2017, when then-Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson created an election infrastructure subsector. The 16 sectors currently designated “critical infrastructure” were given that label under a directive from President Barack Obama.

AI increasingly seems to meet the definition of critical infrastructure, which the law says is “so vital to the United States that the incapacity or destruction of such systems and assets would have a debilitating impact on security, national economic security, national public health or safety, or any combination of those matters.”

The researchers say there are novel threats in the AI industry.

Some of those threats are popping up in other “critical infrastructure" sectors. Last month, federal officials warned of an “active threat” to manufacturing, energy, water, chemical, food and commercial facilities sectors from AI-powered hacking efforts targeting industrial control equipment.

AI infrastructure has also been a target for military action. During the U.S.-Iran war, Iranian drone strikes hit Amazon data centers in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates, causing damage that affected banking operations and destroyed data.

Anthropic, OpenAI and Google did not respond to questions about whether they would support a critical infrastructure designation.

Designating AI as critical infrastructure under CISA would require action from the president, from Congress or both.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment. But Trump has already directed CISA to create a “cybersecurity clearinghouse” and coordinate research on software vulnerabilities and assessments of new AI models. And recently, he said he plans to appoint a czar to oversee an “AI Force.”

Stephanie Justice, a spokesperson for Americans for Responsible Innovation, said that could be a path toward a designation.

“Now that President Trump has discussed his plans for an AI Force, we urge him to use this new body as a way to secure AI as a critical infrastructure,” she said.

That level of interest hasn’t quite reached Capitol Hill.

“I haven’t given that thing any thought,” said Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Arizona) when asked if he would support such a move.

“I don’t know about that,” said Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Missouri). “That’s an interesting question.”

entries.title: Capitals Training Camp Just Started. And It’s Almost Over.
entries.summary: The NHL’s new schedule makes for a fast training camp — leaving the Caps with a brief window to integrate their big-name newcomers and make some tough roster calls.
entries.content:
Training camp started last week for the Capitals. It’s already nearly over.

Such is life now in the NHL. The new collective bargaining agreement has brought a new schedule — a longer regular season, with 84 games up from the classic 82, which comes with a shorter training camp and shorter preseason. For a team like the Capitals, who made several big acquisitions over the summer, that leaves a relatively brief window to integrate a bunch of new talent and make some tough roster calls.

“There's some big decisions that are going to come that we just have not had a lot of game action to evaluate,” Capitals coach Spencer Carbery told reporters on Wednesday. “That's the landscape we're in now with the new CBA. … You just have to make the best decision possible with the information that you have, but it’s more difficult, no doubt.”

In previous years, NHL teams generally had three weeks of training camp with six preseason games. Now, that’s down to two weeks of camp and four preseason games, with restrictions on game action for veteran players. (Anyone with 100 or more career NHL games can now appear in only two preseason games.) That means less time for player evaluation and fewer opportunities to see those players in action. Around the league, teams have adjusted by inviting fewer players to camp and making cuts more quickly. The groups that hit the ice on Day 1 of training camp have generally been the same groups that will make the final rosters for their squads on Opening Night.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

The Capitals will have a few roster decisions to make around the fringes of their depth chart. But their core is already clear — which means their main challenge in this shortened training camp is building team chemistry. After missing the playoffs last year, Washington used the summer to shore up its roster. The front office acquired three forwards: Alex Tuch, Jordan Kyrou and Boone Jenner, and a defenseman, Vincent Desharnais, all of whom are projected to be key contributors.

“With camp being so short, you want to get that chemistry right away,” said Jenner, who spent the first 13 seasons of his career with the Columbus Blue Jackets. “It’s a little different, for sure.”

Much of the team got an early start on that process. It’s no longer common for players to roll into town immediately before the start of camp — many come early for optional summer training and informal group skates. “I think most guys were here the last couple of weeks to try to build some chemistry,” Capitals center Dylan Strome said on the first day of camp. “And to see all the guys and the new faces.”

The beginning of training camp is simply the end of a lengthy offseason prep window.

“There’s no more old-school, drink-beers-in-the-summer-and-show-up-out-of-shape,” said Capitals forward Tom Wilson. “You hit the ground running.”

But no matter how much work the players do individually and in small groups, there is no substitute for playing actual games, even if only preseason games. Particularly for a team attempting to integrate several new players.

Carbery specifically called out the line combination of Tuch and Wilson with Pierre-Luc Dubois as one to watch more closely.

“I need more viewings of that,” Carbery said. “Especially in game action.”

The Capitals acquired Tuch from the Sabres in a sign-and-trade deal in June, agreeing to an eight-year, $84 million contract. He’s spent much of his NHL career playing right wing. But on a roster with several established options, Carbery has started out putting Tuch on the left, where he forms a physically imposing line with Dubois at center and Wilson on the right. (All three players are 6’4”.) They saw their first game action together in the Capitals’ preseason loss to the Bruins last Sunday.

“They’re just getting used to each other,” Carbery said. “They’re trying to read off of one another, and sometimes that happens very, very quickly, and sometimes it takes a little bit more time to learn that.”

They will get some more preseason work this weekend. (The Capitals rematch with the Bruins on Friday before facing the Flyers on Saturday.) If the line isn’t clicking the way they hope, “We’d ideally like to find that out sooner than later,” Carbery said, though he added that he does not want to read too much into limited action.

“I’m going to give those guys an opportunity to see if there’s something there,” Carbery said. “This isn’t like a one-game trial for the line and then blow it up.”

And the window for preseason trials of any length is closing either way. They begin the regular season in just seven days.
