entries.title: Collins' Bipartisan Push to Lower Insulin Costs Likely Won't Get a Vote Before Her Election
entries.summary: Lawmakers are searching for a bill to get through the chamber before the midterms that addresses affordability.
entries.content:
Senate Republicans only have a few working days before they skip town until after the election, and are unlikely to pass any legislation that deals with skyrocketing costs and affordability.

That’s not stopping lawmakers from lobbying to get their bills on the floor — especially the ones they’d like to campaign on.

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who is trying to hold on to her seat in a "toss-up" race, wants to see her bill to lower insulin prices move through the chamber as soon as possible.

“I'm encouraging the bill to be brought up,” Collins said of its prospects ahead of the midterm elections. “It's completely bipartisan and it would make a big difference to a lot of people.”

For now, Senate leadership has not included the bill in its list of major priorities before November. The upper chamber has spent most of this past week debating a bill to establish a national framework for college athletics.

“I think a lot of people are pitching bills,” Collins said of Senate leadership’s response to the request to vote on her bill.

The legislation, which would cap monthly insulin costs at $35 for people with private, employer-sponsored insurance, passed the Senate Health Education, Labor and Pensions Committee by a vote of 17-5 in July. The bill would also establish a pilot program to cap insulin prices for people without insurance in 10 states. It comes as Americans continue to grapple with the cost of living as gas prices reach record highs amid the war in Iran. Collins co-sponsored the legislation with retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-New Hampshire) and Sens. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana) and Raphael Warnock (D-Georgia).

In Maine, around 10% of Affordable Care Act enrollees dropped their coverage in 2026 due to spiking premiums. The Democratic candidate in the state, Troy Jackson, has hammered Collins on the cost of living throughout his campaign.

When asked about the agenda for the remaining week of the Senate’s session, Senate Majority Leader John Thune said that leadership is considering a number of bills, but emphasized that moving onto any new legislation might be difficult.

“There are a couple of things that would be good candidates if you are looking at something that reinforces that message,” Thune said when asked about affordability legislation the Senate could possibly consider. The Ratepayer Protection Act, a bill that deals with costs stemming from data centers “is for sure front and center on that list, and that’s why we are teeing it up.”

The insulin bill went unnamed despite there seeming to be a groundswell of support for it.

Co-sponsor Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) said it “would be great” to see the bill passed before the midterms and Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Missouri), who has also signed onto the bill, said the measure would “absolutely” be a win for Republicans.

But its supporters see little chance of the bill passing before it’s time for Republicans to leave Washington. Sen. Jim Justice (R-West Virginia) said “everybody here is running to get home.”

Justice lamented the fact that Republicans are on the defensive in this election, given spiking costs across the country. He said Republicans should have had a better finger on the pulse of what voters were thinking heading into November.

“We’ve got all kinds of diabetes, all kinds of issues and everything. To get the costs down, it's going to help a big sector of the folks,” Justice said of the bill.

Kennedy said that Republicans have not done nearly enough to tackle the cost of living ahead of the midterms. He told reporters that he has repeatedly expressed to leadership that it’s a shame that Republicans “haven’t done a damn thing” about affordability in 2026.

“It should have been brought up a long time before now,” Kennedy said of the insulin bill.

Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Alabama), another co-sponsor, agreed that there’s simply not enough time to get the bill done ahead of the election. But, he said, senators defending their seats should get back in their states to campaign rather than turning to an entirely new bill.

“Sure it would,” Tuberville said of whether passing the affordability measure before the election could help Republicans. “That’s not going to change a lot of people’s minds. But it would be good to get it done for the people. I don’t worry about the politics part.”

A Democratic aide familiar with the conversations around the bill said that the Trump administration seems “eager” to move the bill forward, emphasizing the idea that the biggest outstanding issue is that Senators are only scheduled to be in Washington for one more week.

Lawmakers are already discussing ways to attach the bill to must-pass legislation like the National Defense Authorization Act or an appropriations measure when they return, the aide added.

“That’s the enemy of the bill right now,” the aide said. “It’s time.”

entries.title: Ketanji Brown Jackson Speaks Out Against ‘Enormously Disruptive’ Emergency Docket Rulings
entries.summary: The Supreme Court’s use of the emergency docket has been criticized for its expedited decisions, oftentimes announced with little explanation.
entries.content:
Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson spoke out this week against the court’s use of the emergency docket, saying that the fast-tracked decisions risk upending the federal judiciary’s order.

The emergency docket is commonly referred to as the “shadow docket” by critics who oppose the court’s expedited, unsigned rulings, often handed down with limited oral arguments or explanations. Use of the emergency docket has become increasingly prevalent under the Trump administration, which has sought immediate relief from lower court rulings while cases make their way through the judicial system.

In Jackson’s remarks, which were delivered to a crowd at the University of the District of Columbia as part of a lecture, she said the emergency docket poses an “enormously disruptive and potentially corrosive effect” on the federal judiciary because it may appear the court is circumventing the legal review process.

“We cannot expect the public to have faith in our judicial system if, without clear explanation, we are consistently green-lighting harmful acts that do real damage to litigating plaintiffs,” said Jackson, a Biden appointee.

Jackson added that the Supreme Court’s current use of the emergency docket is a departure from previous approaches.

“It has been noticeably less restrained, especially with respect to pending cases that involve controversial matters,” Jackson said.

Jackson made similar remarks in a July 16 appearance at a research university in Alaska, where she said it was a “net negative for the court to be evaluating issues on the emergency docket.”

Under the current Trump administration, the emergency docket has provided relief in cases involving the Pentagon’s ban of transgender service members, employee firings by the executive branch and terminating Temporary Protected Status for certain immigrants.

Justice Elena Kagan, an Obama appointee, acknowledged concerns about the use of the emergency docket while speaking at a congressional hearing in July, but she added that the court has elaborated on its decisions when appropriate.

entries.title: A Remarkably Simple Plan to Get the Nats Back to the Playoffs
entries.summary: And yes, it involves fixing the damn bullpen.
entries.content:
Between now and the time MLB begins its next regular season, the Washington Nationals only need to do two things. Add one good starting pitcher. And fix the damn bullpen.

Then the Nats make the playoffs next year.

Probably.

By adding three pitchers — none of them great, but all just MLB-average at their jobs — the Nats should reduce their runs allowed by 70 or more.

All things being equal, that will boost the Nats’ run differential next year to about plus-80, the level which usually equates to 90 wins — and a playoff spot. We’ll “run the numbers” later, but they’re basic.

Ownership, with a payroll the size of a tip jar, can afford it. With the last $35 million of Stephen Strasburg’s deal off the books, the Nats now have zero “albatross” contracts. Their ’27 salary obligations are less than $70 million, according to Baseball-Reference.

No Nat is likely to make $10 million next season, not even CJ Abrams, who recently joined Alex Rodriguez and Bobby Witt Jr. as the only shortstops in MLB history with 30 homers, 30 steals and 100 RBI in a season. Abrams recently accommodated the Nats by moving to second base, presumably so Seaver King (in ’27) or Eli Willits (in ’28) can upgrade shortstop for years. It shouldn’t hurt CJ’s market value. How many 30-30-100 second basemen have existed? One: Alfonso Soriano who did it twice as a Yankee.

If the Nats don’t act this winter, when such sensible spending on two-to-three-year contracts to pitchers can produce such outsized results, then fans may want to emulate ownership next season and spend very little money on the Nats.

My working assumption, based on the recent four-year, $47 million contract extension with staff ace Cade Cavalli, plus a team option at $23 million to keep him in ’31, too, is a sign that the Lerners understand that the time is ripe.

Rarely have I looked forward to the offseason of a Washington team so much. True, the owners will almost certainly lock out the players before New Year’s Day. But MLB, which killed the ’94 World Series, has never canceled a whole year. MLB won’t go full suicide pact with the players this winter, either. They’ll be back.

The Nats’ job is to be ready when they are.

To win 90 games, which makes you a contender, though not a powerhouse, you need to outscore your foes by about 80 runs. As a rule of thumb, for every additional nine runs that you outscore the league, you'll finish one more game above .500. Over several seasons combined, this formula is very precise. It's worked for a century. Of course, in any one year, you can be a half-dozen wins lucky or unlucky. (This year, the Nats have been six losses "unlucky." They're due.)

But that’s how you build your roster.

With three games to play, the Nats have a plus-seven run differential, which is a huge 221-run improvement in one season.

That’s especially amazing because they did it while using the Sisyphus Method. Their bullpen was the boulder. The eighth and ninth innings were the mountain. Sisyphus always got his boulder to the top, then it rolled down. But he wasn't hurt. The Nats? Forty-two times the boulder crushed ’em.

This year, from the eighth inning onward, the Nats have allowed 230 runs in 297 innings. Their ERA is 6.33. This much scoring should be impossible in a parent-pitch youth league. But the Nats have done it.

Luckily, in MLB, the bigger the problem, the easier the solution — or the first steps to a solution, anyway. Why? It should be child’s play to improve from “horrible” to merely “very bad.” You can even improve from horrible to "poor" quite fast.

What would that mean for the Nats?

The Angels are 25th in ERA from the eighth inning onward. Yet they’ve only allowed 181 runs — 49 fewer than the Nats! The 20th-ranked team (still poor) has allowed 161 runs — 69 fewer than the Nats.

A Nats bullpen in ’27 that ranked in that 20th to 25th range in the late innings — talk about a low bar for a team with money to spend — would have a fine shot at cutting runs allowed by 60. That alone might put the Nats in MLB's 12-team playoffs next year.

If you want to fantasize about an “average” bullpen in the late innings (with a 3.97 ERA), the Nats might allow 85 fewer runs than in ’26.

The Nats don’t need a whole new bullpen.

They only need two new relievers. A closer and a set-up man. Those two pitchers would work about 150 of the 300 or so innings that every team has from the eighth inning onward in a 162-game season. But they'd work a large majority of those innings when holding a narrow lead. Also, their presence would put all the Nats’ young relievers in less stressful roles more appropriate to their abilities and experience.

By asking less, you’d get more out of solid, established Brad Lord and … let me think, there must be somebody else … OK, probably Orlando Ribalta. Though their sample size is small, MLB’s Baseball Savant metrics also project Will Dion, Riley Cornelio, Erik Tolman and Jack Sinclair as useful relievers (4.00 ERA, give or take), though not stars.

The Nats are proud that in the last two months they've brought up "bigger arms" from the minors with higher ceilings. As a group, they are also very wild young arms. Don't squash ’em with pressure.

The Nats shouldn’t overrate their own prospects, or their ability to coach them up. It's a common mistake. I’ve dug into spin rates, induced break, first-strike percentage and all the rest. Some may blossom; but for '27, they need help. If the Nats repeat '26, fans may hold their own Boycott-for-a-Bullpen Night.

The addition of a starting pitcher is also obvious. This year, the Nats hoped Zack Littell, Miles Mikolas and Jake Irvin could be “innings eaters.” They ate ’em, all right — 330 of them with a 5.40 ERA.

The average MLB starter has an ERA in the 4.20s. Right now, the ’27 rotation may be Cavalli, Connelly Early (from the Curtis Mead trade), Andrew Alvarez and two question marks. One answer may be DJ Herz, who's now back from Tommy John surgery after having a fine rookie season in '24 with a 4.17 ERA and 10.74 strikeouts-per-nine innings in 19 starts.

But that’s just not enough. Any winning team knows that a solid five-man rotation requires eight starting pitchers! You’re gonna need ‘em.

Last year, Littell fit the profile — a sturdy 30-year-old with a 3.95 ERA over the two previous years. He flopped. Pitchers are unstable isotopes. You take your chances.

So, try again.

One more solid starter stabilizes your rotation, eats innings and takes pressure off your bullpen. How many fewer “runs allowed” does this fellow generate? Probably 20, at least.

Nats fans can sense what a ton of fun was lost this season, courtesy of the bad pitching, with a team that’ll probably finish third in MLB in runs, first in steals, first in extra-base hits, second in total bases and fifth in home runs.

The Nats have had a stunning load of good news in president Paul Toboni’s first year, from the ascension of Cavalli (who stayed healthy for 32 starts), Daylen Lile (who may be a speedster with power and a good leftfielder, too) and Jacob Young (who raised his OPS by 123 points), to catcher Keibert Ruiz reviving his career while playing a well-rested 105 games instead of an exhausted 135.

But, ironically, the best news of ’26 is how awful the bullpen was and how often the "innings eaters" were an eyesore.

The Nats have the youngest every-day players in MLB, average age 24.7 years old. They have one of the top-rated minor league systems with plenty of trade pieces. They are almost overloaded with bats. Rookie manager Blake Butera and his staff seem to have the ear of the clubhouse despite the blown saves.

The Nats need to understand how close they probably are. Not to a title. But to having a playoff team with a sound foundation. Don't keep waiting and dawdling. If you won't step up to support your own players, and your fans, then don't buy an MLB team.

Someday, there’ll be an offseason for an incredibly bold move, like the Max Scherzer signing.

But not this winter. This is the easy one. Do the obvious. And expect large dividends.

entries.title: Pope Leo XIV Responds to Trump's Press Ban
entries.summary: A reporter asked the pope for his thoughts on the president barring outlets from the White House.
entries.content:
By Nicole Winfield

ABOARD THE PAPAL PLANE — Pope Leo XIV told reporters they were welcome to cover him, as he responded to the Trump administration’s attempt to bar U.S. media from the White House and affirmed the importance of journalists covering public figures.

Leo spoke to reporters Friday on his way to France for a four-day visit. Asked by a CNN reporter about the Trump administration’s attempt to bar CNN and other reporters, Leo said the media was welcome on his plane.

“I am very happy that here, you are all welcome,” he said. Good media coverage is important, he said, and equally important "that we have it all the way around, for everyone”

CNN, MS NOW and Politico were back at the White House on Thursday after a judge handed them a reprieve from President Donald Trump's ban, but the extraordinary showdown between him and outlets whose coverage he dislikes continued.

On a high-profile day when Chinese leader Xi Jinping was visiting Washington and attending a state dinner, no major American network was airing live coverage, and both CNN and MS NOW said their journalists were denied access to Xi’s state dinner arrival.

Leo has long affirmed the need for free and independent press, a point he made in one of his first audiences as pope. Speaking to journalists who covered the 2025 conclave that elected him, the American pope called for the release of imprisoned journalists and affirmed the “precious gift of free speech and the press.”

That said, since the COVID-19 pandemic, independent media have been prevented from covering photo opportunities inside the pope's private studio when visiting heads of state visit. Additionally, many of the pope's private audiences with other groups and individuals are closed to non-Vatican press.

Leo Had Opposed Trump on the War

Leo's airborne comments about Trump followed his April back-and-forth over the American president's criticism of his opposition to the Iran war. The American pope's position won him points with some Europeans opposed to Trump's policies.

“He dared, at his level, to oppose the American president,” said retiree Thierry Marien, who lined up hours early to grab a spot on the popemobile route to Notre-Dame cathedral, where Leo was to celebrate vespers later Friday. “Not because he is opposed to the American president but because he’s opposed to countries where we can see there’s a risk of their political systems becoming a bit more dictatorial and there are already enough of those in the world.”

“I appreciated that he did that. He could quite easily have said to himself, ‘In my situation, I won’t criticize any heads of state,'” he said.

Leo Apologizes to Reporters

Also on the flight Friday, Leo also apologized for missing an opportunity to speak with the press the last time he traveled internationally, when his Iberia charter broke down in Spain's Canary Islands and he returned home solo on the king's private jet, skipping his traditional airborne press conference.

More than 70 reporters and the Vatican delegation waited for several hours at the airport for a replacement plane to arrive. Leo addressed the media's disappointment when he came to the back of the plane to greet reporters.

“A special mention I would like to make for those of you who were traveling with me when we returned to Rome from Spain,” he said. “I want to apologize personally for an incident, that I had nothing to do with, but which I know left a number of you unhappy with the fact that we couldn’t have the flight back together back to Rome.”

In other comments to reporters, Leo said he believed his alma mater Villanova would be the fan favorite when the Augustinian university plays Notre Dame's basketball team in Rome on Nov. 1.

“They tell me that the people coming to the match, 90% are Villanova and 10% Notre Dame, so the voice of the people of God will be very strong on the Villanova side,” Leo said.

Associated Press writer John Leicester in Paris contributed to this report.

entries.title: Anxiety Remains High for East Potomac Park’s Future
entries.summary: On a tour of the park Thursday, Rep. Don Beyer and local advocates called for transparency about renovation plans.
entries.content:
The battle for the future of East Potomac Park continued on a quiet Thursday as Rep. Don Beyer toured the area with local advocates, continuing their call for clarity on changes to the park.

The group, which included representatives from the Washington Area Bicyclist Association and the Cherry Blossom Ten-Mile Run, walked the length of the park to Hains Point, pointing out trees removed by the Trump administration and a general lack of transparency they feel the administration has provided about the changes.

Regular patrons of the park sitting in cars, fishing and jogging watched the tour curiously. As the group approached Hains Point, a bicyclist reminded them that they were walking in the wrong lane.

“So many people come out to the park to use it,” said Arlington resident LeRoy Hansen, a legally blind cyclist who often rides a guide-led tandem bike around the park and was part of the tour. “On nice days, people are out here waxing their cars.”

Advocates have raised the alarm for months about the uncertainty of renovations the Trump administration wishes to make at the park, to no avail.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum published a rendering of the park on social media in May that depicted updated amenities on the golf courses while still displaying public recreation areas. A few weeks later, President Donald Trump was photographed with renderings of the park that did not include any public access points or retain Ohio Drive.

“This is a perfect … all right, not perfect, it's a great public space,” said WABA Executive Director Elizabeth Kiker. “If you have plans to change it, maybe it'll make it better. But can you show it? Can you talk to us about it? Can you tell us what the plan is?”

The outcome of any future renovations of the park remain unclear. The National Park Service has begun issuing contracts to vendors for work in the park, including for the fortification of the seawall. Trump said in June construction of a championship golf course would begin this month. However, attorneys for NPS and the Interior Department said only necessary tree removals have occurred.

Beyer (D-Virginia), who grew up in D.C., said he had been coming to East Potomac Park for more than 70 years and played golf on the courses as a teenager. “It's been very concerning to me as a member of Congress right across the river, because so many of the constituents who live in Northern Virginia use this park every day and every year,” he said.

He questions whether fill that sits on the golf course after being removed from the East Wing of the White House contains arsenic, lead or other toxic materials that pose a risk to recreational park users. “We learned today that it's been seeded over. I've done enough construction. I like to know that when you get toxic materials, things should be buried deeply someplace, not left on top at the low grass level,” he said.

Beltway Golfer Magazine publisher Alex Dickson, who was part of the group, is a plaintiff in a lawsuit against the Interior Department and the National Park Service to ensure the golf course and recreational areas remain publicly accessible. Soil testing data from NPSindicated that toxic materials were present in fill material at rates potentially harmful to wildlife and human health. Plaintiffs in that case filed an amended complaint last week that challenged the quality standards of the initial testing and why the material would be used as fill in a public recreation area.

“The levels of toxicity in those reports, it's not just about the golf course. It's not just about getting your dirt in your golf clubs and sand traps and being used for the future golf course, but it's going right into the local waterways,” he said.

The government is expected to file a response by Oct. 9. In the meantime, Beyer and the local advocates are hoping to secure a meeting with the superintendent of the National Park Service in the capital region.

"What we really need to do, as we've heard that there's no trust, is to rebuild that trust," Beyer said. "We start by having honest, forthright conversations with the leaders of the Park Service, and perhaps up the line to Doug Burgum at Interior and the White House itself."

entries.title: Iran Outlines Seven-Day Plan to Bring Hostilities With the U.S. to an End
entries.summary: “We are not in a rush,” a U.S. official told The Washington Sun.
entries.content:
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said this week that the country’s leaders had submitted to the U.S. a seven-day plan to end hostilities.

Araghchi, who mentioned the plan while speaking to reporters in a briefing at New York’s United Nations General Assembly Thursday, said Tehran is ready to negotiate a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and a cessation of hostilities, which have been going on and off since February.

“We have introduced a plan to the United States through the intermediators that if certain conditions are met, the Strait of Hormuz would be open on the end of the seventh day, and talks would restart,” Araghchi said.

The seven-day proposal resembles a previous agreement struck between the U.S. and Iran in June, and was communicated through conflict mediators. Tehran’s new proposition aims to fast-track negotiations and end the conflict, which has now stretched on for more than six months.

A U.S. official confirmed to The Washington Sun the Trump administration is “having positive and constructive discussions through the mediators,” while arguing that the U.S. has a lot of leverage over Iran.

“The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz, so we are not in a rush. Over the last 48 hours, nearly 40 million barrels of oil have transited the Strait,” the official said.

The June proposal was short-lived, as both sides accused one another of violating parts of the agreement, and came as both nations’ heads of state delivered aggressive speeches during U.N. interventions.

The plan would also include possible talks about Iran’s nuclear program, Al Jazeera reported, which President Donald Trump has repeatedly cited as a major reason as to why the war began in the first place.

“Will a deal be made with Iran?” President Trump said on Tuesday, “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”

In an interview with Fox News’ Bret Baier, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian defended his country’s posture.

“We did not choose war; the war was imposed on us,” Pezeshkian said on Thursday. “We're seeking an agreement if the counterpart agrees to it.”

Iran’s seven-day sequence would begin with a halt to hostilities across the Middle East, including in Lebanon, alongside the lifting of the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports, the removal of sanctions on Iranian oil exports and the release of at least $12 billion in frozen Iranian assets.

If those conditions are met, Tehran says it would reopen the Strait of Hormuz on the seventh day, after which the U.S. and Iran would resume negotiations over a longer-term agreement, including Tehran’s nuclear program.

entries.title: Xi Says He’ll Meet With Trump Twice More This Year
entries.summary: The promise of more meetings to come capped off a three-day state visit that has been criticized by some in the U.S. for being heavy on pomp and light on substance.
entries.content:
By Michelle L. Price and Fu Ting

Chinese President Xi Jinping wrapped up his state visit to Washington on Friday by announcing that he expects to meet President Donald Trump two more times before the end of the year, doubling the number of face-to-face discussions between the leaders of the world’s two largest economies in 2026.

The promise of more meetings to come capped off a three-day state visit that has been criticized by some in the U.S. for being heavy on pomp and light on substance, though Trump said they discussed the war in Iran. The two leaders have made a show of working to preserve harmony, but there were no major breakthroughs this week on issues such as trade or the safety of artificial intelligence.

Xi extended an invitation for Trump and first lady Melania Trump to go to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, in November and noted that they could meet again a month later at the G20 summit at the Trump National Doral Miami golf club in Florida.

“We do welcome Mr. President and the first lady to visit China,” Xi said.

Trump responded, “We will, and we’ll be speaking a lot.”

Trump took Xi to the National Archives

Trump on Friday took Xi to visit the National Archives, showing off the sacred texts of U.S. democracy to the leader of the world’s most powerful communist country.

Trump, a Republican, has been seeking to demonize Democrats as communists during the run-up to the November midterm elections, a message that has been muddied by the red-carpet treatment he has given Xi this week.

The visit comes as the U.S. celebrates the 250th anniversary of its founding.

The Archives has a special exhibit marking the semiquincentennial, titled “The American Story,” which highlights the country’s accomplishments and advances, along with images depicting its darker moments.

Trump showed Xi one copy of the Declaration of Independence on Thursday — a wall-mounted copy he keeps in the Oval Office.

Inside the nation’s vault of records, where the Declaration of Independence, the U.S. Constitution and the Bill of Rights are held, Xi peered at the documents that are kept under protective glass as a guide spoke about them.

After viewing the Constitution, Trump told reporters waiting nearby that the two leaders discussed how old their nations are.

“We’re just comparing,” Trump said. “Ours goes 250 years, which is great, and we’re proud of it. But theirs goes 6,000 years.”

He added: “There’s a little difference between 6,000 and 250, but we’re very proud of our 250.”

The leaders and their spouses also had tea in the Red Room

Xi's day began at the White House, where Trump and the first lady hosted the Chinese leader and his wife, Peng Liyuan, for tea in the White House’s Red Room.

Their visit fell during China’s Mid-Autumn Festival, a national holiday when families traditionally gather to celebrate the end of harvest, sharing mooncakes, round pastries filled with a sweet paste, over tea.

Xi thanked the Trumps for the visit. "The highest courtesies, the most meticulous arrangements,” Xi said in Chinese. “This visit is very successful, and we also feel very satisfied.”

Trump grinned when an interpreter relayed what Xi had said.

“We’ve had a tremendous visit from two spectacular people, and we really enjoyed it, and I think we’ve made tremendous strides,” Trump said. “We’ve made great strides, very positive for both countries.”

Xi enjoyed a state dinner and a White House tour

The Trumps feted their guests Thursday night with a black-tie state dinner attended by technology industry titans. Earlier in the day, Trump gave Xi a personal tour of his White House flourishes, including a gallery wall of presidents and a new 100-foot-long (30-meter-long) granite helicopter landing pad — and pointed out his ballroom, still under construction. Melania Trump and Peng Liyuan toured the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Asian Art.

The two leaders also met behind closed doors for 90 minutes on Thursday, when they discussed issues such as the Middle East, Ukraine and the Korean Peninsula, according to the official Chinese government readout of the meeting.

The White House has not provided any information about the private talks, but Trump told reporters at the Archives on Friday that he and Xi discussed the Iran war in their meeting. He did not offer additional details.

“We had a great meeting. We had a really great meeting. Great for the farmers. Great for everybody," he said.

Outside the building, the two leaders said goodbye and exchanged one last handshake before getting into their respective cars. Xi was set to leave Washington, and Trump returned to the White House.

entries.title: Trump Says Scott Bessent Will Not Be Named ‘AI Czar’
entries.summary: The president put to bed speculation that the Treasury secretary is in the running to be the White House’s next AI czar.
entries.content:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will not be the next AI czar, President Donald Trump announced Friday, leaving the coveted White House role open as the AI industry’s rapid development becomes a leading policy issue in Washington.

The announcement followed reports that Bessent was a front-runner for the job after taking a leading role in the administration’s AI policy.

“Scott Bessent will not be going to be Super Intelligence (SI) Czar. Number One, he doesn’t want to. Number Two, he’s doing such a great job at Treasury, and that’s where I want to keep him! Why would I ever make such a change? Just more Fake News!” Trump wrote in a TruthSocial post.

Bessent oversees the exploding sector’s impact on the economy from his perch at Treasury.

The previous crypto and AI czar, David Sacks, vacated the position in March. He currently co-chairs the president’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.

entries.title: Federal Appeals Court Rejects Anthropic’s Challenge to Pentagon Blacklist
entries.summary: The ruling does not reverse a separate decision last month that struck down other administration actions against Anthropic.
entries.content:
A federal appeals court rejected Anthropic’s challenge to a Pentagon decision labeling the artificial intelligence company a national security supply-chain risk Friday, handing the Trump administration a legal victory in its monthslong fight with the company.

“The Department had ample support for its conclusion that the continued integration of Claude into the Department’s information systems, by the Department or its contractors, presented a statutorily covered national-security risk,” reads the ruling from the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals in its 2-1 decision.

The court pointed to Anthropic’s ability to build restrictions into its models and previous instances in which Claude refused tasks requested by government users.

The dispute began in February, after negotiations between Anthropic and the Pentagon broke down over the department’s demand that its Claude models be available for any lawful purpose, including uses that conflicted with the company’s restrictions on mass domestic surveillance of Americans and fully autonomous weapons.

But the Friday ruling does not reverse a separate decision last month that struck down other administration actions against Anthropic.

“We respectfully disagree with the court's decision,” an Anthropic spokesperson said in a statement to The Washington Sun. “Another federal court has already held the government's parallel designation unlawful. We remain confident in our position and are considering all options, including further review.”

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Defense Department designated Anthropic a supply-chain risk under two federal laws, leading to separate court challenges for each.

One designation, issued under a Pentagon-specific law known as Section 3252, was part of Anthropic’s broader lawsuit against the administration in federal court in California. U.S. District Judge Rita F. Lin struck down that designation in August, along with other administration actions aimed at cutting off Anthropic from federal work.

The Pentagon also designated Anthropic a supply-chain risk under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act, a separate law governing risks to the federal government’s supply chain. Anthropic challenged that designation directly in the D.C. Circuit.

The appeals court also directly addressed Lin’s ruling. It said the law at issue in her case has a narrower definition of a supply-chain risk that required evidence of bad intent, while the law at issue in Friday’s decision does not.

The court acknowledged that Anthropic imposed its restrictions over concerns about privacy and AI safety, rather than an intent to harm the government. But it said Anthropic’s motives did not matter in this case.

The law, the court said, “turns on what Anthropic does, not why Anthropic does it.”

entries.title: Supreme Court Allows States to Purge Voters Using an Updated Immigration Database
entries.summary: The high court ruled that states can again access to a modified version of the SAVE system to check for noncitizen voters despite critics’ privacy concerns.
entries.content:
The Supreme Court on Friday cleared the way for states to use the federal government’s overhauled immigration database to purge noncitizens from voter rolls ahead of the midterms.

The unsigned decision sided with the Department of Homeland Security, which sought to revive the modified system — which contained Social Security information and other individual data — after U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan ordered it shut down in June. Three justices dissented from the decision.

While the court acknowledged arguments that the updated database violated privacy laws, it said Congress had already authorized DHS to request and receive citizenship information from other agencies like the Social Security Administration in a 1996 immigration law provision.

Blocking the modified database would put other agencies in an “impossible predicament” of having different laws requiring different disclosures, the order says.

“It is improbable that Congress intended to place officials in such a bind when it passed the IIRIRA,” the justices wrote, referencing the 1996 law that reshaped immigration proceedings.

One section of that law, signed under President Bill Clinton, “appears to contemplate an information-sharing regime like the modified SAVE program,” the decision says.

DHS had updated its Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, database — meant to track the status of immigrants in the country — after President Donald Trump issued a March 2025 executive order aimed at rooting out potential noncitizen voters.

Expanding the database by adding personal data and new features prompted a lawsuit over concerns that the Social Security number search feature constituted a privacy violation — amid broader concerns that the database could have inaccuracies that would lead to American citizens being erroneously flagged as ineligible to vote.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, in a dissent joined by Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan, wrote that the majority opinion “focuses only on the harms the Government will purportedly suffer absent a stay, disregarding the harms that the modified SAVE system has caused, and will likely continue to cause, to lawful voters.”

The legal battle over the modified database exemplified the complexities behind implementing Trump’s aggressive — and often legislatively fallible — push to cut down on noncitizen voting, which is already an extremely rare occurrence.

A federal appeals court ruled against the government on Sept. 4, citing DHS’s forfeited arguments rather than weighing in on whether the department had violated the Social Security Act. The updated database remained disabled following the 2-1 decision.

In its request for the Supreme Court to revive the database, DHS argued that the plaintiffs, a group that includes several states and the League of Women Voters, could not show they were directly harmed by SAVE rather than decisions made by individual states.

The older system undermines the goal of voter-roll maintenance and works too slowly for use during the midterms, government lawyers argued, also knocking down arguments that the addition of SSNs violated privacy laws.

The League of Women Voters argued in a response brief filed Tuesday that it is too late to redeploy a modified system that several Democratic states have characterized as unreliable and inaccurate, citing the National Voter Registration Act’s “quiet period” that mandates a 90-day limit on systematic purging before federal elections.

In its Friday decision, the court’s majority said performing “individualized inquiries” using the modified database is permissible within the 90-day limits, and that the district court’s earlier decision “inhibits” the federal government’s efforts to assist local agencies in administering midterm elections.

Sooknanan’s ruling had coincided with another federal judge’s order to revive the system in a separate case involving four states that sued DHS to get the department to reinstate the updated features for their use.

The Supreme Court also recently halted the U.S. Postal Service from proceeding with a rule to tamp down mail-in voting ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms, and Trump administration lawyers have also faced a so-far-unsuccessful attempt to obtain copies of states’ voter rolls.

entries.title: Commanders GM Says Jayden Daniels Won’t Go on Injured Reserve
entries.summary: “As of right now, surgery is not on the table, and we haven’t discussed IR,” Adam Peters said Friday.
entries.content:
Commanders general manager Adam Peters said that the team doesn’t expect star quarterback Jayden Daniels to need surgery on his injured elbow, and that there hasn’t been any discussion about placing him on injured reserve.

In a Friday morning appearance on “The Sports Junkies” on 106.7 The Fan, Peters said the team is trying to make the right medical decision to get the former Heisman Trophy winner back on the field this season.

“He just got back late last night, this morning, and we met with doctors, and it’s just a matter of thinking what the next best course of action is,” Peters said. “As of right now, surgery is not on the table, and we haven’t discussed IR. So it’s just a matter of how we're going to get him back on the field.”

Daniels dislocated his left elbow on the final play of the first half in the Commanders' 37-20 Week 2 loss to the Cowboys in Dallas. He dropped back under center on a third-and-goal situation, stumbled and planted his left arm on the field before shoveling an incomplete pass to the sideline.

“It wasn’t good,” Peters said, describing his initial reaction to the injury from the press box. “It wasn’t poised. It wasn’t cool, calm and collected.”

Peters said when he went to see Daniels after the game, he felt a lot better about the situation. He said Daniels had handled the situation “extremely well” and “definitely different than the last time.”

Daniels injured the same elbow in a 38-14 loss to the Seahawks last season, which sidelined him for seven of the team’s remaining eight games.

“I think he’s just as frustrated as anything else because he was playing so well,” Peters said. “Once I saw him and talked to him, he probably calmed me down more than anything.”

Before Sunday’s injury, Daniels had thrown for 96 yards and a touchdown and led the team on the ground with 69 rushing yards on seven carries.

entries.title: Trump’s ‘Paid for by the U.S. Government’ Ad Campaign Draws Scrutiny
entries.summary: “It feels like Viktor Orbán,” Sen. Thom Tillis said.
entries.content:
A campaign-style advertisement, apparently funded by taxpayer dollars, that features images of President Donald Trump over a music track titled “Love Me” is raising eyebrows on Capitol Hill and beyond.

The video, which has a duration of about 30 seconds and first aired Wednesday on Newsmax and Fox News, features the president pledging to fight communism, socialism and Marxism in the United States, while touting his administration’s tax cuts, manufacturing policies and law-enforcement efforts.

Over half a dozen Democratic lawmakers, including Sens. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire and Jack Reed of Rhode Island, as well as Reps. Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut and Steny Hoyer of Maryland, have called for the video to be pulled.

“The advertisement does not have a clear official government purpose and appears to run afoul of federal prohibitions against the use of appropriated funds as part of ‘a general propaganda effort designed to aid a political party or candidates,’” Hassan said in a letter directed to the White House chief of staff, Susie Wiles.

The advertisement, which ends by stating that it was “Paid for by the U.S. Government,” has also been criticized by Republican senators, with some even describing the ad as "inappropriate," and comparing it to the style of Hungary’s former prime minister and longtime right-wing leader.

“It’s not like they need a GoFundMe page to have the dollars to do that sort of ad, and they could do it. But using taxpayer dollars, it feels like Viktor Orbán,” Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina told reporters.

Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana also questioned the video’s legality. 

“I don’t generally like to see politicians use public money to pay for their own campaign ads,” Kennedy said.

The cost of airing the ad in local markets across the country has cost the government at least $430,000, according to AdImpact, an organization that tracks media spending.

Outside Capitol Hill, at least one nonprofit has asked government watchdogs to conduct a thorough investigation of the ad, which is described in a letter to the U.S. Government Accountability Office and the U.S. Office of Special Counsel as potentially in violation of federal law.

“Public Citizen is filing this complaint seeking appropriate investigation and enforcement actions by the Government Accountability Office and the Office of Special Counsel,” the organization, a think tank dedicated to protecting consumer rights, said in the letter.

“Whether or not President Trump was personally involved in the ad, it was conceived, produced and distributed by Trump’s White House staff,” the letter states.

The R&B artist whose song was featured on the ad, JMSN, also suggested on social media that the administration had used his song without permission.

“I would never authorize my music to be used for ANY political agenda or campaign,” JMSN, whose real name is Christian Berishaj, posted to X on Thursday.

In a statement to The Washington Sun, a spokesperson for the Trump administration did not address lawmakers' concerns, saying instead that the ad is “educational” and “unapologetically patriotic.”

“These public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad,” the spokesperson said.

A White House official also said the “[public service announcements] are clearly not political,” and that President Trump is not on the ballot.

This is not the first time the Trump administration has come under fire for federal spending on advertisements.

In March of this year, a $220 million ad featuring then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem sparked bipartisan criticism of the administration’s use of taxpayer dollars for political-style messaging.

entries.title: White House TV Pool Is Operating Again After Days of Outlets Being Banned
entries.summary: When the White House booted CNN and two other outlets from the grounds, the other four networks in the pool declined to participate in a show of solidarity.
entries.content:
By Jocelyn Noveck

The U.S. network video pool for the White House was back in operation Friday, for the first time since President Donald Trump banned three news outlets in a high-profile showdown over media access.

“As of now, all systems are go,” said a person familiar with the pool, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the fluidity of the situation.

The pool consists of five major U.S. broadcast outlets that take turns shooting and sharing video. When the White House banned CNN — which belongs to the pool — and two other outlets from White House grounds, the other four declined to participate in a show of solidarity.

A judge temporarily struck down the ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico on Thursday, but his ruling didn't directly address the pool. The networks continued to refrain from covering Trump as part of the pool even as reporters from all three outlets were allowed back in the White House.

As President Donald Trump prepared to take Chinese President Xi Jinping to visit the National Archives on Friday, the pool's live feed was being shared again.

CNN was not commenting directly on Friday, referring instead to its editorial coverage. But Brian Stelter, the network’s media analyst, posted on X that CNN had a pool assignment at the National Archives event and that the White House had approved the network’s credentials.

A daily White House press schedule listed CBS as one of the pool assignments Friday. CNN also had a pool assignment Friday, and an Associated Press journalist saw the network preparing on site.

entries.title: Senators Tell Trump to Uninvite Putin From the G20 Summit
entries.summary: Lawmakers from both parties say hosting the Russian president would give him “stature and legitimacy” as his war in Ukraine rages on.
entries.content:
A bipartisan group of senators is pressing President Donald Trump to withdraw Russian President Vladimir Putin’s invitation to the G20 summit later this year in Miami.

The 13 senators, including six Republicans, warned that welcoming Putin to the United States would give him “stature and legitimacy” while Russia continues its war in Ukraine.

“We urge you to reverse course and rescind the invitation to President Putin,” the senators wrote.

The letter was signed by Republican Sens. Roger Wicker (Mississippi), John Cornyn (Texas), Thom Tillis (North Carolina), John Curtis (Utah), Jerry Moran (Kansas) and Alan Armstrong (Oklahoma), and Democratic Sens. Jeanne Shaheen (New Hampshire), Michael Bennet (Colorado), Richard Blumenthal (Connecticut), Chris Coons (Delaware), Ruben Gallego (Arizona), Tim Kaine (Virginia) and Sheldon Whitehouse (Rhode Island). Wicker chairs the Senate Armed Services Committee, while Shaheen is the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

The senators also called on the administration to bar other sanctioned Russian officials from upcoming G20 meetings until Russia agrees to what they called a “just and lasting peace” in Ukraine.

The G20 leaders’ summit is scheduled for Dec. 14-15 in Miami.

The White House and State Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio publicly confirmed the invitation Wednesday after meeting Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Rubio said the summit would give Putin an opportunity to engage with Trump and other world leaders.

The letter comes days after Trump signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, giving the administration new tools to increase economic pressure on Moscow.

The senators praised Trump for signing the law but questioned whether inviting Putin to a major international summit undercuts that pressure.

“If President Putin and his government are not isolated on the international stage, what incentive does Russia have to agree to a ceasefire?” they wrote.

The senators also objected to other Russian officials having attended G20 meetings in the U.S. earlier this year.

They pointed to sanctioned Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov’s participation in a finance ministers meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, along with Russian delegations at meetings in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, and Houston.

Putin and Siluanov are both sanctioned under Executive Order 14024, which targets harmful Russian foreign activities. The senators argued that allowing sanctioned Russian officials into U.S.-hosted G20 events gives Moscow “business-as-usual treatment” while the war continues.

entries.title: Afternoon Sun: Pain in the Ads
entries.content:
THE LATEST

Donald Trump’s first campaign-style advertisement — which states it was “paid for by the U.S. Government” — drew scrutiny from both parties this week over its legality and messaging. The administration reportedly paid at least $443,000 to air the “Love Me” spot across the country.

  • “Using taxpayer dollars, it feels like Viktor Orbán,” Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) told reporters.
A new spot dropped this morning, also narrated by Trump and presented as paid for by the government, featuring multiple sweeping shots of Mount Rushmore and American landscapes. Administration spokespeople repeatedly insisted that the ads are “public service announcements” and do not contain political or campaign themes.

  • “This is only the beginning of the golden age of America,” Trump says in the second ad.




THE ADMINISTRATION

Scott Bessent will not be the president’s new AI czar, Trump announced on Truth Social, following reports the Treasury secretary was a front-runner.

The State Department will propose a rule expanding election officials’ and nonprofits’ access to sensitive passport data to conduct voter checks.

Iran’s foreign minister said the country’s leaders have presented the U.S. a seven-day plan to end hostilities. The proposal resembles a previous agreement struck from June.





THE COURTS

The Supreme Court cleared the way for states to use the federal government’s overhauled immigration database to purge noncitizens from voter rolls ahead of the midterms.

  • Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson spoke out this week against the court’s use of the emergency docket to fast-track decisions.
A federal appeals court rejected Anthropic’s challenge to the Pentagon’s decision to label the AI giant a national security risk earlier this year. The panel pointed to Anthropic’s ability to build restrictions or refusals into its models.

Another federal appeals court appeared reluctant today to force the administration to bring back the Venezuelan men it deported to El Salvador’s notorious CECOT prison.





THE STATES

Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell resigned from his position in New Jersey today after an ethics investigation concluded he made sexually explicit comments to a staffer. He has denied the allegations.





THE HILL

After Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-New Mexico) publicly asked Apple and Google to maintain his state’s name — which Trump said he could change to “New America” — on their mapping services, the senator’s office said neither company expressly committed to keeping the current name.

  • Google said its Maps product is informed by “relevant local and regional determinations,” while Apple said it takes its data from the Geographic Names Information System, Luján’s office wrote in an email.

entries.title: Trump Forgoes Battleground Rally Promise for a Red State Tour
entries.summary: Trump's itinerary is yet another sign of the uphill fight that his party faces.
entries.content:
By Jill Colvin and Kim Chandler

MONTGOMERY, Alabama (AP) — President Donald Trump vowed to campaign in 35 of the most competitive battleground districts in the final sprint to November's midterm elections.

Instead, he will begin October by stumping in Alabama and Oklahoma, two of the most Republican states in the nation. His events are sure to draw enthusiastic crowds of fans, but his choice of destinations is a reminder of his deep unpopularity in much of the country during a campaign season he's sought to make all about himself.

Trump will hold rallies next week in Durant, Oklahoma, and Mobile, Alabama, where he is sure to draw crowds, but has also raised eyebrows.

While organizers insist the rallies are in locations with media markets that span state lines and they will help bolster broader turnout, Trump's itinerary is yet another sign of the uphill fight that his party faces. Republicans have already been pouring money into red states once considered safe as they try to shore up candidates facing an unhappy electorate that has soured on Trump and his polices.

Some Republicans have also been distancing themselves from the president in recent weeks as they as they try to appeal to voters beyond Trump's “Make America Great Again” base. They're removed or downplayed references to the president on their websites and increasingly voiced opposition to his unpopular war with Iran.

But Trump's events — Thursday in Durant and Friday in Mobile — are also likely to deliver something else he craves: adoring crowds. He is almost guaranteed to fill the venues with the kind of die-hard supporters who fueled his political rise, projecting excitement as he tries to bolster enthusiasm and rally Republicans.

“The President’s ability to engage with and activate low-propensity voters is unmatched. That’s why he’ll be barnstorming the country to activate the voters we need to win in November,” said Republican National Committee spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre, promising more October rallies to come.

Democrats, meanwhile, celebrated the announcement. “The political floor is falling out from underneath Trump and Congressional Republicans, forcing them to scramble to spend and campaign in deep red territory in the final weeks,” said Viet Shelton, spokesperson for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

The RNC noted that Durant, Oklahoma is on the Texas border and next to the Dallas-Fort Worth media market, and will draw Republicans in Texas, which has emerged as one of the most critical states on the map. Scandal-plagued Attorney General Ken Paxton, whom Trump backed over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn, is locked in a tight race against Democrat James Talarico. Gov. Greg Abbott is also facing a stronger-than-expected challenger in Democrat Gina Hinojosa.

Mobile is next to Florida’s panhandle, a Republican stronghold where high turnout can help bolster Trump-backed candidates running for Senate and governor. However, Florida Republican Sen. Ashley Moody is not expected to attend.

In Oklahoma, Trump will be stumping for Mike Mazzei, whom he backed as the Republican nominee for governor during a competitive primary. Mazzei is running against Oklahoma's Democratic House Minority Leader Cyndi Munson.

“This race continues to get more competitive – and national Republicans are right to be worried about Mazzei,” Democratic Governors Association spokesperson Kevin Donohoe said in a statement.

Alabama, meanwhile, holds deep nostalgia for Trump and his early supporters. He held his first mega-rally in Mobile more a decade ago, drawing some 30,000 people to a college football stadium. The crowd made clear to skeptics of his campaign that he was more than a celebrity novelty.

“I think it’s very natural that he would host a rally here as he is gearing up for the midterm elections,” said John Wahl, the Republican candidate for lieutenant governor and former chair of the Alabama Republican Party.

Although Republicans remain the heavy favorites in Alabama's statewide campaigns, they face a more challenging political landscape this year.

Former Democratic Sen. Doug Jones is mounting a vigorous campaign for Alabama governor against one of Trump’s most vocal allies, Republican Sen. Tommy Tuberville, who said he welcomed the president's visit.

Republican Rep. Barry Moore, running to replace Tuberville in the Senate with Trump's backing, said the president's rally “will be the jet fuel we need to win big in Alabama.”

Mobile is also near Alabama's 2nd Congressional District which leans red after its lines were redrawn but is not a slam dunk for Republicans as they try to dislodge Democratic Rep Shomari Figures.

Figures has been criticizing president's plan to lower import tariffs on foreign beef in an appeal to cattle ranchers as he tries to fend off a challenge from his Trump-backed opponent, State Rep. Rhett Marques.

Trump has promised to ramp up his campaigning in the election's final stretch and had said he would visit all of the most competitive districts .

“It’s all about 35 races,” he said at a recent Rose Garden dinner attended by Republican lawmakers. “I’m going to go to every one of those 35 places and we’re going to see if we can get everyone elected."

entries.title: Results From AI Talks Go MIA as Xi Departs D.C.
entries.summary: Technological innovation and its risks were a hot-button issue heading into the week, but it’s unclear how much was discussed between the world leaders.
entries.content:
China’s leader, Xi Jinping, left Washington on Friday afternoon after a whirlwind visit to President Donald Trump’s White House. And while Trump leaned into the personal nature of the leader-to-leader relationship and showed off the White House’s renovations — some completed and some ongoing — the status of what the bilateral negotiations produced on key issues between the adversaries remained largely unknown.

“We've had a tremendous visit from two spectacular people. And we really enjoyed it,” the president said Friday morning, seated for tea with Xi, his wife and first lady Melania Trump.

U.S. officials signaled in public comments a breakthrough on some tariff relief between the two countries and Chinese agricultural purchases, which they expect to announce next week. It’s confirmation that the central focus of the U.S.-China relationship continues to be trade.

“When the president visited China in May, we agreed on the vision of building a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability. This time, we've agreed to add new substance to it,” Xi said through an interpreter. Trump later added that America’s farmers will be “very happy.”

The president confirmed that he and Xi discussed Iran, as China continues to support Tehran.

But artificial intelligence and whether the U.S. would push China to address the growing safety concerns loomed over the anticipated meeting. Now at the end of Xi’s visit, few details have emerged from either side. And the dearth of information is unlikely to silence the president’s critics and could disappoint Trump’s allies who seek stronger federal regulations — and were hoping Trump would push China on it, too.

Trump said he and Xi spoke about the subject in a “very productive meeting,” but summarized the conversation in superficial terms.

“He seemed to like calling the poorly and inaccurately named Artificial Intelligence to a far more accurate and important name, SUPER INTELLIGENCE,” the president wrote in a Truth Social post.

There is a reason for the emphasis on personal touch over substance, said Sara Schuman, a former senior U.S. negotiator for China trade and managing director at Beacon Global Strategies.

“The relationship between the two is still in a competitive mode. And Trump views himself as a backstop to managing the tensions,” Schuman said.

Few former or current officials and experts who The Washington Sun spoke to expected a major breakthrough on the issue. But fanning out on cable television, Trump officials highlighted the establishment of a “dialogue” between the two countries, a proposal that was announced days before the official meetings started, as the summit’s most tangible result.

“What we talked about is developing a dialogue,” David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, said in an interview Friday morning on CNBC. “We reaffirmed that here. We’ve established this dialogue and also a crisis mechanism between the two countries … That’s historic.”

That dialogue will be managed by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, among others.

The Trump administration sought to tamp down expectations of breakthroughs on the AI conversations ahead of and during the talks. Bessent, who has taken a leading role on AI for the administration, told Fox News on Wednesday that the U.S. would “define with them what we think the most important or the most perilous risk factors are." While the president cautioned in a Thursday social media post that “Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is,” he added that the only guardrail will be the Justice Department, though it’s unclear how it would regulate the growing industry.

The president is expected to meet with major tech companies, alongside House Speaker Mike Johnson, next week to discuss the way forward.

Trump’s resistance to calls for more dramatic regulation of AI is an aim to keep America’s AI capabilities superior to China’s, according to sources familiar with the White House’s thinking who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private deliberations.

“They want to see the U.S. [as] the global leader in AI,” an industry source familiar with the administration’s AI priorities told The Sun. But how the country maintains that edge — including innovating with the fastest chip processors and physical hardware for AI models — in a way that satisfies critics remains unclear. “What regulatory regime is necessary to achieve it?” the source asked.

And there’s concern within the White House, according to sources familiar with discussions, that if the U.S. slowed down its AI development and elicited from the Chinese an agreement to do the same, the Chinese couldn’t be counted on to follow through.

While Xi talked on Thursday about managing AI development responsibly, a gulf exists between the approaches of China’s AI leaders and American companies that’s rooted in a disagreement about the severity of risk posed by unchecked AI innovation.

American AI leaders have increasingly warned the American public about the dangers of rapid AI breakthroughs. The idea that AI might pose an existential threat to mankind is less of a topic among Chinese policymakers, said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center.

“There is a gap in perceived risks of AI, and there’s a big gap between the U.S. AI industry and what we’ve now seen recently with the fears that AI could kill us all in the next decade, and a lot of views in China,” Chan said. “Ironically, their views actually kind of match up a little bit more with Trump’s.”

Trump’s more laissez-faire approach has maintained tension between some industry figures and the president about how best to balance innovation with regulation, as well as within the administration itself. While Trump remained firm on his pledge not to stifle AI, White House aides were prepared to confront Beijing over the alleged theft of U.S. AI models by Chinese companies — though by the time Xi departed, it was unclear if that confrontation happened.

Those following this issue closely say there is a lack of understanding and consensus from the White House and Congress on the goals for AI regulation, and without that, it’s difficult to make uniform demands from China.

“You gotta start somewhere,” said a former Trump official, who specialized in China trade. “I do think eventually there will be agreements around it, but this will be the first conversation. I don't know if it's gonna be that useful a conversation because I don't think [regulations] have been worked up in a way that would allow each side to develop a clear position.”

A second former Trump official said ahead of the summit that they were watching to see “any potential relaxation of export controls,” specifically around chips, as the real barometer of progress.

“I think the degree to which there are any potential relaxation of export controls coming out of the meeting will be a real sign as to whether or not there's been any meaningful discussion on that topic,” said the official.

Greer poured cold water on that notion in a Friday interview with CNBC. The chips, which Greer called “the crown jewels of American technology,” haven’t been part of the trade negotiations.

“It’s the way we stay ahead in the race for, you know, superintelligence or AI, and so those conversations actually — they’re not really happening in these negotiations,” Greer said. “All those export controls that are national security issues, we take those off the table.”

And as with most policy debates, Trump's whims guide the ultimate outcomes.

“What we’ve experienced is that policy runs through the White House,” the industry source said. “Different parts of government have different points of view — predictably, because they’ve got different responsibilities — and then it’s the Oval Office synthesizing that and giving guidance.”

Trump, Xi and their respective delegations could have two more chances this year to deepen discussions on AI, as Trump is expected to visit China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders' Meeting in November and Xi is expected to return to the U.S. for December’s G20 summit, which will be hosted at one of Trump’s Florida properties. Still, it’s unclear to many when and if the two superpowers can find a reasonable solution on AI as China races to supersede the U.S. as the premier world power — a push that is, in some ways, powered by its technological innovation.

“[The] Chinese government will have their own definition of ‘responsible,’” the industry source said, calling the continued dialogue between the nations “in and of itself, a victory.”

entries.title: New Jersey Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell Resigns After a Sexual Harassment Investigation
entries.summary: Caldwell said he stepped away from his post so as not to distract from the administration.
entries.content:
New Jersey Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell resigned Friday after a blistering ethics investigation concluded he made sexually explicit comments to a staffer and tried to use his position to secure a state job for his girlfriend.

On Thursday, Gov. Mikie Sherrill gave her second-in-command 24 hours to post his resignation in the wake of the 61-page report by investigators for an outside law firm. Caldwell has denied the allegations.

“I’m not resigning because of the report,” he told The New York Times. “It’s false. I’m resigning because I don’t want to be a distraction to the administration.”

The governor’s ethics office opened the probe into Caldwell after officials received an anonymous tip in May alleging that the lieutenant governor had sexually harassed a young woman who worked for him.

According to the report, Caldwell, 66, made a sexual remark after a staffer told him her friend was not interested in a relationship with him. Caldwell responded that the staffer and her friend “needed a man who was in a position to help them,” but that "you young women are looking for young sperm."

Investigators from law firm Lowenstein Sandler concluded that Caldwell’s behavior constituted sexual misconduct and ethics violations.

Caldwell’s lawyer, Thomas Calcagni, pushed back against the report’s findings and called into question the credibility of the staff member.

“This unnecessarily protracted and one-sided process lacked the requisite due process that should be afforded every citizen of this state,” he wrote in a document refuting the report.

Investigators said that four days after Caldwell received notice of the ethics probe, he used his government email to advocate for his girlfriend to receive a promotion to a state government job. They also uncovered evidence that Caldwell brought guests to several ticketed events without payment, despite receiving explicit warnings from ethics officials.

Sherrill held a news conference about Caldwell’s resignation Friday afternoon. She said he underwent a “thorough” vetting process before the two were elected on the same ticket and took office in January, but his behavior after taking office raised concerns and justified the ethics probe.

“Public servants must abide by the highest ethical standards,” she said. “We can no longer tolerate the culture of silence, sweeping things under the rug or kicking cans down the road.”

Sherrill said her team will work to hire a new lieutenant governor over the next 45 days, and she intends to prioritize someone with a history of “focusing on the public good.”

entries.title: Trump Administration Proposes Using Passport Data to Conduct Voter Checks
entries.summary: The State Department proposal to expand election officials and nonprofits’ access to passport records is highly unlikely to take effect until after the midterms.
entries.content:
The Trump administration proposed granting federal and local election officials, as well as nonprofits, access to sensitive passport records to conduct voter citizenship checks.

The State Department proposal, first reported by Bloomberg News on Friday, would explicitly add “voter eligibility” to the list of uses for which the department maintains passport records. The plan lists federal, state, tribal and local government agencies, along with unspecified nonprofit organizations, as potential recipients of passport data.

The proposed rule is highly unlikely to take effect until after the Nov. 3 midterms, though it combines with President Donald Trump’s ongoing push to assert federal authority over maintaining state voter rolls to remove noncitizens — a campaign his administration says is necessary to prevent voter fraud, which is extremely rare.

The records system at the center of the State Department’s proposal stores Americans’ sensitive personal documents, including passport applications, birth certificates, copies of driver’s licenses, and medical and financial data.

The draft notice specifies that data can be shared with the government and nonprofits “for the purpose of verifying the identity or citizenship for users accessing government websites and applications, voter eligibility, and other governmental services,” but falls short of specifying which nonprofits or government agencies would receive the passport records, or which records they would receive.

The Privacy Act allows records to be shared for narrower purposes, like law enforcement and employment verification and identity checks, but voter eligibility is not a listed use. However, the Supreme Court on Friday allowed the government to move forward with its modified immigration database, which contains citizens’ Social Security information and other individual data — despite an earlier lower court ruling that found that the updated system violated federal privacy laws.

Earlier this week, the Justice Department informed a judge of the new State Department plan as part of an ongoing legal battle over Trump's March executive order seeking to curb mail-in voting rules. A federal district court had explicitly ordered the DOJ to update it on any "material factual developments" while the litigation remains pending.

The State Department has already notified the relevant congressional committees of the proposed passport data sharing provisions, according to the DOJ’s disclosure to the court.

The State Department proposal will soon be published to the federal register and eventually undergo a 30-day public comment period.

entries.title: Appeals Court Weighs Whether the U.S. Should Bring Back Venezuelans Sent to CECOT
entries.summary: Two of the judges on the panel seemed hesitant to require the government to return migrants flown to CECOT.
entries.content:
A federal court appeared reluctant on Friday to force the Trump administration to bring back the Venezuelan men it deported to a prison in El Salvador.

A three-judge panel for the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals heard arguments on whether dozens of Venezuelans sent to El Salvador’s notorious Terrorism Confinement Center, known as CECOT, should get hearings to challenge the legality of their removal.

U.S. District Judge James Boasberg previously ordered the federal government to return the Venezuelan nationals, saying the administration flagrantly violated the migrants’ due process rights when it labeled them members of the Tren de Aragua gang and rapidly deported them. The men have since been released from CECOT and are back in Venezuela, though some have fled to other countries.

The appeals panel seemed less sure about bringing the deportees back. Two judges on the panel — Circuit Judges Neomi Rao, a Trump-appointee, and Raymond Randolph, appointed by former President George H. W. Bush — said that bringing the immigrants back to the U.S. would return them to detention when they’re already free in Venezuela.

“They’re not in custody now, and if any one of these individuals decides to show up at the border they would be in custody, and that’s the remedy,” Randolph said.

Lee Gelernt, the American Civil Liberties Union attorney representing the Venezuelans, said the court could not allow the government to dump people in a prison in a foreign country without giving them the opportunity to get relief.

“There are some we can’t find because they're in hiding in Venezuela,” Gelernt said. “We will find them eventually, but it’s not as if they’re released and they’re walking around in a free country.”

The government argued that it didn’t have control over the deportees when they were in CECOT. Now that they have been released, there’s nothing the U.S. government can do, Justice Department attorney Tiberius Davis said.

“Obviously the people were released to Venezuela, they’re either free or have traveled to other countries, nobody contends that we have custody over them, and I think that that certainly shows that the case is moot here,” Davis said.

Circuit Judge Harry T. Edwards, appointed by former President Jimmy Carter, criticized Davis’ argument that the Trump administration didn’t have custody of the migrants.

The oral argument marked the next phase of the legal battle that is all but certain to end up back at the Supreme Court. In April 2025, the justices gave President Donald Trump approval to carry out the removal of Venezuelans under the Alien Enemies Act, but stipulated that the immigrants have a chance to challenge their deportations.

Next week, the entire D.C. appeals court will hold a hearing on whether Boasberg can pursue a contempt investigation against Justice Department officials for ignoring his order to turn around a flight taking migrants to CECOT. Rao, who was part of Friday’s panel, was one of the appellate judges who stopped Boasberg’s contempt inquiry in April.

“These two cases will collectively decide whether the rule of law is going to remain strong in this country or whether the Trump administration is going to get away with violating court orders and thumbing their nose at the courts,” Gelernt told The Washington Sun before the hearing.
