entries.title: Ranchers Criticize ICE Raids for Disrupting Livestock Operations
entries.summary: “These types of disruptions will lead to higher beef prices for consumers,” groups from three states say.
entries.content:
Livestock producers from Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas are criticizing Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids that are shutting down or slowing critical meat-processing facilities.

The Kansas Livestock Association, Texas Cattle Feeders Association and the Oklahoma Cattlemen's Association released a statement Friday that the raids are disrupting their workforce and will result in higher prices for consumers.

The raids are primarily centered in the Kansas cities of Garden City, Dodge City and Liberal, but have caused concern across the livestock industry. Ranchers frequently travel hundreds of miles to move cattle to a processing facility.

Scarlett Madinger, vice president of communications of the Kansas Livestock Association, said that ICE’s actions have caused employees to stay home. That has created a backlog of cattle that need to be culled and processed, she said, forcing ranchers to spend extra money transporting the cattle back to their feed yards.

Along with the meat-processing facilities, local businesses across southwest Kansas closed temporarily. Madinger said ICE’s operations have “gotten out of hand” and created mass disruption and fear throughout southwest Kansas.

“These ICE operations are having a massive chilling effect on the legal, documented, skilled workers that put beef on the table and keep the cattle supply chain moving,” the three livestock associations said in the press release. “Additionally, these types of disruptions will lead to higher beef prices for consumers.“

The livestock groups made those comments as several Republican candidates in competitive races are criticizing the Trump administration’s immigration agenda.

The immigration operation has hit an industry already stretched thin. The nation's cattle herd has been shrinking for years, and the number of beef cows is at its lowest point in decades. Ranchers are producing fewer calves each year, and industry analysts expect supplies to stay tight into 2027.

Ground beef hit a record of roughly $7 a pound this summer, with beef prices rising more than twice as fast as overall inflation. The Trump administration has tried to ease the squeeze by opening the door to more beef imports, a move that upset ranchers.

ICE’s actions have upset local leaders and drawn criticism from Kansas’ Republican senators.

“Law enforcement officers were not given advance notice or the level of cooperation we would expect from ICE’s enforcement and removal operations. As a result, there have been mass disruptions to local communities and businesses,” Sen. Roger Marshall said in a statement.

Sen. Jerry Moran said he spoke with the Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and that DHS was only targeting those with criminal warrants. However, representatives from the livestock associations say mass raids have occurred.

entries.title: SCOTUS Strikes Down GOP-Set Missouri Congressional Maps
entries.summary: The decision by the court preserves Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver’s Kansas City district for the midterms.
entries.content:
Missouri’s congressional map is finally set for this year’s elections — after voting has already started.

The Supreme Court cleared the way for the state to use its 2022 map on Friday, ruling against Republicans who targeted a Democratic-held seat in a redistricting push. It was the third time this month the Supreme Court ruled in a way that left the state using the older map, and almost certainly the last.

The unsigned order comes as voting in the general election in Missouri is already underway, with in-person absentee voting having started on Tuesday and ballots having been sent out to eligible out-of-state voters as early as last Friday.

“Given this Court’s two prior orders in this litigation, our conclusion that this was error should come as no surprise,” the order says.

And the court did not mince words for lower courts. “The District Court and Court of Appeals should not enjoin or otherwise prohibit the use of the 2022 map in the 2026 congressional election in Missouri,” the order says. “And the District Court and Court of Appeals should not order or otherwise require Missouri to use the 2025 map in the 2026 congressional election in Missouri.”

Republicans had sought to redraw Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver’s 5th District seat, splitting Kansas City into three congressional districts and likely giving them a 7-1 map.

The ruling from the Supreme Court ensures that Cleaver will keep the same district lines as prior years, where he is highly favored to win in November.

Missouri was one of the first states in which Republicans redrew their lines last fall after President Donald Trump asked state lawmakers to make maps more favorable to the party ahead of a tough midterm year.

The drama over Missouri’s congressional maps has spanned four courts over the past year. The Missouri Supreme Court ruled that Denny Hoskins, the secretary of state, must use the 2022 map for the midterms, and the Supreme Court declined to halt it.

Then, in a separate case, a federal district judge ordered state officials to use the redrawn map. The Supreme Court halted that order. A federal appeals court on Monday gave new life into the party’s push for the more GOP-friendly map, ruling that the new map should be used unless the Supreme Court steps in within a week.

People Not Politicians, the advocacy group leading the effort against the Republican redistricting push, quickly appealed on Tuesday night. The Supreme Court did so Wednesday.

Hoskins and the two Republican candidates had argued that Missouri voters shouldn’t have to vote for different candidates than they did in the primary, and that candidates shouldn’t have to run in different districts.

“Represenative Onder and Mr. Brattin each won their August primary under the district lines the 2025 map drew, and the 2022 map would force each of them to stand for election in November before a substantially different, non-consenting electorate,” lawyers for the plaintiffs wrote Wednesday afternoon.

entries.title: White House Releases Second ‘Paid for By the U.S. Government’ Ad
entries.summary: The administration maintains that the advertisements are “public service announcements.”
entries.content:
The White House released a second government-sponsored broadcast advertisement on Friday claiming the U.S. is the most successful nation in history amid growing bipartisan backlash over the apparent use of taxpayer dollars to fund the spots.

“Liberty has prevailed here because of the culture and character of the people who declared it, defended it and preserved it,” President Donald Trump’s voice narrates in the latest advertisement video, accompanied by footage of Mount Rushmore and Trump’s July Fourth speech. “We know that this is not an ending. This is only the beginning of the golden age of America.”

It is still unclear how much the government spent on the second ad, but the newly released minute-long video has at least aired on Newsmax’s “Carl Higbie Frontline” and “Greg Kelly Reports” shows, according to ad tracker AdImpact.

The first ad, called “Love Me,” dropped Wednesday and has cost at least $443,000, per AdImpact.

Administration spokespeople said the videos — labeled “Paid for by the U.S. Government” — are considered “public service announcements” with the goal of educating Americans to be “unapologetically patriotic.” The White House doubled down on its message through an official press release Friday afternoon, saying that past administrations, dating back as far as President Woodrow Wilson, had used the airways to inform the public.

“When prior Administrations utilized the airwaves, it was called ‘public education.’ When this Administration promotes pride in our country, many of those same voices call it ‘propaganda,’” the statement read.

The two advertisements prompted sharp bipartisan criticism from lawmakers and calls for investigations into the administration's federal spending on political ads, just over a month before this year’s midterm elections.

“The advertisement does not have a clear official government purpose and appears to run afoul of federal prohibitions against the use of appropriated funds as part of ‘a general propaganda effort designed to aid a political party or candidates,’” Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-New Hampshire) wrote in a letter to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles on Thursday, referencing the first advertisement.
